speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GUARANTEED MINIMUM MONTHLY INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier, in the house, I indicated the government's intention to provide a further program of income support for older persons in Canada. I promised members I would give the house a general outline of this program before we adjourned for the summer. I am pleased to carry out that commitment, but before I do there are a number of comments I would like to make.
First, I believe the action taken earlier by this house in approving the Canada Assistance Plan will be of real assistance to many older people. Also medicare, when it comes into effect, will bring substantial benefits; indeed, it will be of special importance to older people, just as hospital insurance has been.
I would also remind the house that since this government took office the flat rate pension has been increased from $65 a month to $75. Some 100,000 persons have been brought under the old age security program this year through lowering of the eligibility age to 69 and in January of next year, when the eligibility age will be dropped to 68, another 100,000 will receive full benefits. This yearly reduction in the eligibility age will continue until 1970 when all persons 65 and over will be entitled to the flat rate pension.
By this time, 1970, the flat rate pension will be available as a matter of right to some one and a half million persons age 65 and over. Also, of course, a steadily increasing level of retirement benefits will be payable under the Canada Pension Plan, commencing next January. The Canada Pension Plan, we feel,
will largely solve the problem of basic retirement pensions when its provisions come fully into effect and pensions are payable at the full scales provided in it. The plan in itself is a generous one.
There are, however, many older people in Canada who cannot benefit fully, or at all, from the Canada Pension Plan, because they are already past the retirement age or because they will be retiring before the plan becomes fully operational. I do not have to remind the house that the position of this particular group has been of considerable concern to this parliament and to this government.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
I would also note the recommendation of the joint committee on the Canada Pension Plan urging further measures on behalf of those people who, because they are or soon will be retired, will not be substantial contributors to or beneficiaries from the Canada Pension Plan.
The increase in the monthly flat rate pension and the lowering of the eligibility age are in line with this recommendation, but clearly this is not all that is needed. I can assure the house that the government, and more particularly my department, has for some time been exploring various additional ways through which adequate assistance can be provided for this group of people. I would recall, for example, a speech which I gave on March 2 in Regina in which this problem was discussed. At that time I noted that a considerable number of older persons would not be able to take advantage of the Canada Pension Plan. I went on to discuss some of the various approaches which were being considered to meet this problem.
It is apparent, then, that a further program of benefits should be considered for persons in this particular age group. We propose to introduce a program that will guarantee a minimum monthly income of $105 to old age security recipients.
The details of such an income guarantee program are now being considered. The total payments which will be required under this program will, of course, decrease over the years, as the Canada and Quebec pension plans come into effect and pay increasing benefits.
July 14, 1966
7652	COMMONS
Old Age Security Income Announced
The program is being provided with these two plans in mind and is specifically designed for those people who are not and will not, because of age, be able to take advantage of the contributory pension plans. This, as I said, is in line with the recommendations of the special joint committee. Because it is an income guarantee program, and because of the increasing benefits that will be available under the Canada and Quebec pension plans, the burden on the federal treasury will be almost entirely a transitional one.
By using the contemporary income guarantee formula rather than the flat rate increase it is felt that income support can be provided at a higher level for a given outlay of funds. Through this income guarantee program the needs of the older citizen can be more adequately met in a way that is financially responsible and least burdensome on the treasury.
I can inform the house that such a program will be presented to parliament for approval in the autumn, after parliament has reconvened.
It is estimated that the annual cost to the treasury of such a program will be in the neighbourhood of $225 million at the beginning. The revenue measures that will be needed to meet the burden which these supplementary benefits will place on our national finances are also being considered.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GUARANTEED MINIMUM MONTHLY INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have listened to the long awaited announcement just made by the minister with some trepidation and disappointment. While it is true the minister says this legislation will be coming before us in the fall for approval, we had hoped to deal with it now.
I should like the minister to explain whether this supplementary benefit will be based on a means test, which is not acceptable, because his statement was not clear in this regard. This announcement comes after a great deal of urging by the party on this side of the house to which I belong.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GUARANTEED MINIMUM MONTHLY INCOME
speechtext: And the Liberal backbenchers.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GUARANTEED MINIMUM MONTHLY INCOME
speechtext:
And as someone has said, there has been some urging on the part of a Liberal backbencher. The government has finally seen the light. It is pleasing to note that we in this party have fought constantly for a pension increase and we are happy that we have succeeded at least to the point of having an announcement, even though the actual increase is still to be delayed.
[Mr. MacEachen.)

This program will bring a measure of contentment and happiness to our older citizens, and in a great many cases it will provide many of the necessities they need so badly when the program comes into effect. As the party which brought this question to a vote early in the session, we are pleased at the result to a point, and are most happy at the measure of justice we hope it will bring to our senior citizens. However, Mr. Speaker, I would ask the minister whether the increase could not be made effective as of now, to help combat the high cost of living.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GUARANTEED MINIMUM MONTHLY INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, any announcement
that indicates that there is to be an improvement in the income of our old age pensioners should be greeted with approval in this House of Commons. However, I must say that the statement the Minister of National Health and Welfare has at long last made to parliament is bitterly disappointing. In the first place, if there is anything in this program that has any value, that offers any help to our senior citizens, it should be put into effect right away.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GUARANTEED MINIMUM MONTHLY INCOME
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GUARANTEED MINIMUM MONTHLY INCOME
speechtext:
It is not good enough to tell the older people of this country that approval will be given in the fall to a measure the effective date of which has not been indicated to us in the statement given by the minister. The crux of this proposal is that there will be made available to our senior citizens an additional amount of money on a different basis from that on which they receive the present $75 a month. The minister uses the phrase "guaranteed annual income". He indicates in his statement that the details are yet to be worked out, but it is clear from such details as he has given us that the plan includes a means test under another name. All the government is proposing is that old age pensioners who do not have $30 a month of other income can qualify for up to $30 a month under this supplementary provision. That is a means test.
The proposed increase will be fine, if you forget the quality of dignity, for those who have nothing else. But there are thousands of older people in this country who, because there has been no means test in respect of the old age pension, have saved a little money and have incomes all told of $105, $110, or $150 a month. These people today are in desperate circumstances. In this legislation there is nothing for them at all. That is why I
July 14, 1966

say that this long awaited announcement, with all the fanfare we have had about it and the pulling of teeth it has taken to get it, is bitterly disappointing.
The minister does not make clear just where Canada Pension Plan benefits fit into this scheme, but I think one can see where they fit. They are to be part of the other income that comes under this means test that the minister calls a guaranteed annual income. The whole concept of the Canada Pension Plan was to provide additional income, and now it is income that is to be taken into account under a glorified means test. The minister makes it clear that this proposal is to be transitional in character. He says the burden on the treasury will diminish as the years go on and the Canada Pension Plan comes into full force. In other words-let us get this clear-this is not an increase in the old age security pension, which is what the people of this country want at this time.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GUARANTEED MINIMUM MONTHLY INCOME
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GUARANTEED MINIMUM MONTHLY INCOME
speechtext:
My friends across the way can groan, but they will really groan when they get back to their constituencies and meet their people when they have learned that this government has tried to fob them off with a supplementary payment which is on a means test basis.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, the parliament of Canada
took one of the greatest steps in its history when it said that retirement income is a matter of right. We did that in 1951 when we removed the means test from the old age pension. To put it back on any portion of what our senior citizens are to receive is a retrograde step, and I hope that between now and the fall when we come back to deal with this legislation the government will repent of this decision and will announce a decision which the people of Canada want. The government will hear about the reaction of the country to this proposal from the hundreds of thousands of people who will not benefit from this measure at all, and I urge the government to reconsider its whole position.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare has let the cat out of the bag by giving us the figure representing what he thinks this plan will cost in the first year. The Minister of National Health and Welfare says that at the beginning it will cost $225 million a year. Since I heard that figure I have not had time to do my arithmetic in
7653
Old Age Security Income Announced precise detail, but I have been able to compute that at best this will amount to an average of $15 a month for the people on our old age pension rolls during the first year.
The government says it is offering a total of $105 a month, which represents a supplement of $30 a month; but on an average, according to the terms of this proposal, it only comes to $15 a month or perhaps even less.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GUARANTEED MINIMUM MONTHLY INCOME
speechtext: It is only $11.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GUARANTEED MINIMUM MONTHLY INCOME
speechtext:
Some of my friends have had more time to do their arithmetic than I, and they are saying it is only about $11 a month. This means, Mr. Speaker, that because some people will get the full amount, many if not most of our old age pensioners will not get any at all.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, although, as I said in the beginning, one would expect that any announcement which does anything for our old age pensioners should be welcomed, this statement is bitterly disappointing. It is not satisfactory from a financial point of view and, what is even worse, it takes away from our senior citizens something that we gave them in 1951-their dignity, and their entitlement to their old age pension as a right. I deeply regret that a government which calls itself Liberal has announced that it intends to come in with such legislation.
The matter of old age pensions, Mr. Speaker, could be dealt with in a direct, straightforward and honest way, and I call upon the government to reconsider its decision. At the end of March, 1966, there was a surplus of $216,982,834.44 in the old age security fund, even after some of the money in that fund had been transferred to another fund. According to an answer given to a question placed on the order paper by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler), the Department of Finance estimated that at the end of the fiscal year in which we now find ourselves, the total surplus in that fund will be $455 million.
In other words, even though we are lowering the eligible age and putting more pensioners on the roll, the surplus in this fiscal year will be greater than the surplus in the last fiscal year. This is money which comes from three taxes, 4 per cent on personal income up to a ceiling, a 3 per cent sales tax and a 3 per cent corporation tax, which were earmarked for the old age security fund by a decision of parliament. The old age security fund is on a pay as you go basis. The money
July 14, 1966
7654	COMMONS
Old Age Security Income Announced which is collected from the taxes paid by the people of Canada and which is being put into the old age security fund is for the payment of old age security pensions, and therefore I say it is a violation of the spirit of that act for the government to leave that money in the fund and not give it to the people for whom it has been collected.
There are over a million pensioners in Canada today. Perhaps there will be 1,200,000 by the time the 68 year olds get on the roll in 1967. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this year every pensioner on the roll could be paid the extra $25 a month that we urged they should receive, could be paid this sum retroactively to the beginning of the fiscal year, could receive the full $300 increase out of the old age security fund, and there would still remain in that fund at the end of the year a surplus of more than $100 million.
It is a disgrace, Mr. Speaker, for the government to come in with the statement that has been made today, in view of the money which is lying in the old age security fund. This money was collected for the old age security pension, collected on a pay as you go basis, but the government has refused to use it. I say that this statement today is bitterly disappointing to us in this house, and it will be received with great disappointment throughout the country as a whole because the people realize that not only is there a need for extra money on which to live, but there is a need for-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GUARANTEED MINIMUM MONTHLY INCOME
speechtext: I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I shall now be concluding my remarks. I urge the government to look at its position in the light of the financial needs of the older people of this country and in the light of the right of our senior citizens to their dignity. We gave it to them in 1951. Let us not take it away by a proposal of this kind.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GUARANTEED MINIMUM MONTHLY INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the announcement made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen), my remarks will be very brief, because I do not find very much to say except to criticize his statement about the increase in the old age pension.
After a great deal of thought and many hesitations, the minister made that statement today, at the very last minute before the adjournment of the present session, and instead of talking about old age security, he preferred to talk about the pension plan. I think therefore, that disappointment will be felt throughout Canada, because Canadians were expecting something else; as far as we are concerned on this side of the house, we would have preferred for our old people more than the crumbs offered by the minister in his statement.
As a matter of fact, the old people are led to believe that they are getting an increase in pension but, if you study carefully the minister's statement, you will find that instead the proposal will take something out of their income.
We saw that the minister succeeded in bypassing an election promise made last fall and we would have been surprised if he had offered us something else at this time.
July 14, 1966	COMMONS
In any event, over the recess we will have the opportunity and time to study more carefully the minister's recommendation and, when the session resumes in the fall, I am convinced that each member will see to it that the minister is made aware of the demands of the Canadian people, particularly those of the old people. I would not like to be in the shoes of the Liberal members who will have to explain the government's decision to their electors.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GUARANTEED MINIMUM MONTHLY INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the announcement we have heard this afternoon is not quite what we have been waiting for. I am reminded of the story which used to be told by the late Solon Low about the farmer who was plowing a field which had a stream alongside it. While the farmer was on the far side of the field his son fell into the stream. As he came round on his tractor and heard the boy screaming he shouted "Hold on while I make another couple of rounds". It seems to me that the old age pensioners of this country are being asked by the government to hold on while the government makes another couple of rounds through the summer.
We have been waiting for some action by the government, expecting that we would receive news of what the papers have been calling over the last few days a generous addition to the incomes of the old age pensioners. But all we have is the promise that the legislation will be presented. Even a member with interests as recent as mine-

speechtext: Why did your party vote against it?

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GUARANTEED MINIMUM MONTHLY INCOME
speechtext: We did not vote against it but afforded the government an opportunity to do something at that time. No one's disappointment is greater than mine at the lack of any specific announcement at this time of any action. One wonders what would happen if the advisers to the Prime Minister were to advise him during the summer to call another fall election, and just how long it would be before the necessary legislation to provide an increase would be implemented.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GUARANTEED MINIMUM MONTHLY INCOME
speechtext: Not much chance of an election.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GUARANTEED MINIMUM MONTHLY INCOME
speechtext:
Somebody says that there is not much chance, and after this announcement I would be inclined to agree; but strange things have happened before.

This is a disappointing announcement. I appreciate the concept we hear of the guaranteed annual income, and I am concerned a bit when the members of the New Democratic Party back away from the concept of the guaranteed annual income every time it approaches. We hear a great deal from them about it at other times during the session, but when it actually comes close to being implemented we see a great deal of fright and a rap.d retreat from what it seems to me must come. The only thing I would say is that if the guaranteed annual income is to b e brought in and is to be successful in its initial and terribly important application, then it must be truly generous, and I do not feel that this increase is truly generous at the present time.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GUARANTEED MINIMUM MONTHLY INCOME
speechtext: You are backing away now.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GUARANTEED MINIMUM MONTHLY INCOME
speechtext:
I do not feel it is generous at the present time. I cannot quite understand the remark of the hon. member in the context of what I have just said.
I know this announcement will be a bitter disappointment to the old age pensioners in this country. I feel the thought which would best sum up their opinions is contained in one of the briefest letters I have ever received from an old age pensioner, which came to me about a month ago. All it said was "Will you lend me $200 till the government gets round to raising the old age security pension?" In that letter there was a sardonic note which I think will prove somewhat justified by the announcement we have had this afternoon.
At a time when every trade union in the country is demanding an increase in the wages of the workers, and at a time when the price index is rising constantly, I urge the government to reconsider this action and if it is at all possible under present legislation, or by order in council after we leave this chamber this afternoon, give a flat increase to the present pension of $75 a month, and then bring in a generous guaranteed annual income in the fall and proceed from there.

subtopic: GUARANTEED MINIMUM INCOME-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: GUARANTEED MINIMUM INCOME-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg leave, pursuant to standing order 26, to move the adjournment of the house to discuss a definite matter on urgent public importance, namely the total inadequacy of the policy just announced by the government which will deprive the senior citizens of Canada of the justice to which they are entitled, and the vital necessity of an alternative which would give an immediate increase of $25 a month to all citizens at age 65.
I plead urgency in the matter because of the critical rise in the cost of living and the position which I have consistently taken in the house this session.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: GUARANTEED MINIMUM INCOME-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Would the hon. member kindly address the Chair on the question of urgency of debate?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: GUARANTEED MINIMUM INCOME-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not want to belabour the house. I made it quite clear that the position I have taken in this regard ever since the beginning of this session is based on urgency and need. As I said before I think it is sufficient for me to say that the critical rise in the cost of living makes my motion urgent and important.
[Mr. Speaker.)
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)

subtopic: GUARANTEED MINIMUM INCOME-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the motion moved by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce makes out a basic case for urgency, in that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has today made his announcement about the government's program to take care of the elderly citizens of Canada.
Throughout the time the house was discussing the Canada Assistance Plan we were assured that some measure would be introduced to take care of the elderly people who are not covered by either the Canada Pension Plan or the Canada Assistance Plan. Only today have we been given some particulars regarding the government's proposal to fill this gap in our social security program. We shall have no other chance to discuss this matter until the house reconvenes some time in October.
It seems to me, therefore, that it is of the utmost urgency that parliament have an opportunity now, first, to express its opinion with regard to this proposal before us and, second, to give the minister an opportunity to tell parliament and the country the specific details of his program. Many old age pensioners, also many hon. members of the house, are still uncertain as to whether they are going to be covered; as to what the effective date will be; as to what will be the conditions employed in determining income; whether income will include alleged rent where a person owns his own home; whether assumed interest on assessed value of property will be taken into account, and whether some of the other factors which made the previous means test so unpopular will remain.
Therefore because parliament will have no opportunity, should it adjourn today, until next fall to discuss this matter, I think parliament ought to have this opportunity now of discussing the measure which the minister has forecast, so the members of this house might be given an opportunity to express their opinions and so the government might have a chance to give us some further information which is sorely needed.

I would ask hon. members to allow the Chair at this point to express its views on the motion which has been presented by the hon.

member for Grey-Bruce. Basically, in spite of the fact that the hon. member refers to a policy announcement which has been made by the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare, the motion is based on a general question having to do with old age security and old age pensions.

I do not think anything could be gained by having further debate on the matter at this time.
Despite the fact that a policy announcement has been made by the minister, the matter before me is the question of urgency of debate. I do not think anything would be gained at this time by having a debate now on the basis of the motion presented by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce.

He was indicating that some of the future plans for procurement of the department were going to be modified, and by way of citing an example he made reference to a contract for bombs to be cancelled, from Canada.
We have since learned that Mr. McNamara had reference in these circumstances, to an intention on the part of the United States Department of Defence not to extend or renew a particular contract for the production of explosives in Canada beyond the

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, July 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Nicholson for the second reading of Bill No. C-215, respecting certain conditions of employment of dock workers at the ports of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this bill was before the house earlier in the week I made a full statement, perhaps too lengthy in the opinion of some people at least, which I trust showed very clearly that in spite of hard bargaining, conciliation and mediation efforts over a period of several months settlement without some action by parliament appeared to be impossible.
I think I might say that on the whole the meetings that took place on Saturday, June 11, and in the early morning of June 12 were constructive and very worth while. With a view to avoiding supplementary statements by some of my colleagues, I wish to summarize the happenings on those two days. On the morning of Saturday, June 11, Judge Lippe and my deputy minister confirmed
July 14, 1966

what the former had said to me the previous day, namely, that the counterproposal of the Shipping Federation of Canada, made a day or two earlier, to the minimum demands of the unions made back on May 26 had been turned down by the unions.
The mediator said to me on the Saturday morning that in his opinion and that of my deputy minister, who had been with him during the last two days of the discussions and mediation proceedings, there was no chance of the parties reaching agreement without some definite assurance to the Shipping Federation, the employer, that they might expect, or might hope at least, for increased productivity, not in 1966, but in 1967, in return for the substantial increases and the assurances of job security that the unions were insisting upon and that he felt that parliamentary action at an early date might be necessary.
I might say that on the previous day the mediator, Judge Lippe, had suggested to me that, to bring the strike to a close consideration should be given to having the three or four remaining crucial issues referred to an industrial inquiry commission, and that the government give consideration to introducing legislation with a view to making binding the findings of such a commission on those three or four matters. Shortly after my discussion with the mediator I conferred with the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and had a meeting with the legal adviser of the Shipping Federation. This was a very brief meeting. I outlined to him briefly Judge Lippe's proposal.
Later the same morning my three colleagues, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Favreau), Judge Lippe, my deputy minister and I met in my office with Mr. Cutler, the legal adviser of the longshoremen's union, and with a few of his clients and Mr. Jodoin, President of the Canadian Labour Congress. At that meeting I first reminded the union representatives-and this had been a cause of complaint on their part and probably a justifiable one-that they now had had for a day or two the counterproposal of the Shipping Federation for which they had been pressing. I then went on to say that since that counterproposal had been turned down there now appeared to be what was described by one of them as an impasse and which I called a deadlock. I said that the government was strongly of the
Labour Conditions
opinion that an early solution must be found.
I then confirmed to the group in my office that I intended, as Minister of Labour, to establish an industrial inquiry commission to look into the working conditions in the three ports and into certain other matters.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I may say that this matter had been under consideration for some weeks, again at the suggestion of the mediator. I then suggested that the possibilities for increased productivity, related job security and other related matters might be referred to the commission for immediate study, and that the other phases of the proposed inquiry into industrial unrest and difficulties on the St. Lawrence, mainly parking facilities on the dock, safety and other matters, might be deferred until later in the year, possibly as a second phase of the study by the commission.
I further suggested that a way out of the deadlock might be found in legislation making the findings of the commission on increased productivity and related matters binding, and that in the same way job security for longshoremen, which was a matter of special concern to the international vicepresident, Mr. Tremblay, might be dealt with by the same commission. I stressed the fact that the strike had been on for over a month and that an early solution must be found even if that solution lay in referring the matter to parliament.
As I have already informed the house, and I want to make this clear particularly in view of an editorial that appeared in the Montreal Star today, Mr. Jodoin, the president of the Canadian Labour Congress, stated he was opposed to compulsory arbitration. We knew that and we appreciate the reasons for labour organizations being opposed to compulsory arbitration, although there might be circumstances when legislation making certain findings binding would be necessary. I might say that Mr. Cutler, the legal adviser of the longshoremen's association, also stated that his clients were opposed to any legislation that would make the findings of the commission binding.
I then put a question to Mr. Cutler in the presence of my colleagues, the deputy minister, Judge Lippe and others. I asked him what would happen if the government were to decide to make the findings of the commission binding in regard to the three or four remaining points-there were 50 or more in the early stages. I mentioned to him that there seemed to be a block to reaching an

July 14. 1966
Labour Conditions
agreement and I wondered what would be their position. Mr. Cutler then said clearly and unequivocally that while his clients were opposed to binding legislation, we could rest assured that they were Canadians and would eo-operate if the government set up a commission. He then said he would advise them on any legislation that might be passed and that they would obey it. There was no question about that. I was not surprised to get that assurance from a fellow member of the bar. I thought it a reasonable statement on his part.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext: But he did not agree.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
True, he did not agree. He told me they were not in favour of legislation which makes anything binding, that it is not in keeping with the principles of democratic labour organizations, or words to that effect. I understood his position. We invited ideas for any solutions and when they were not forthcoming I reiterated that legislation might be the answer.
At about that time the Minister of Transport had been studying a memorandum which contained the counterproposals of the Shipping Federation to which I have referred. He proposed to the International Longshoremen and to their solicitor in the presence of the president of the Canadian Labour Congress that to bring an end to the dispute and to get the men back to work, the strike having lasted for over a month by this time, the government was in fact prepared to introduce legislation, which would ensure that the conclusions of the commission on these three or four crucial points would be made binding-and this proviso was very clear-provided the International Lonshore-men's Association and the Shipping Federation could reach an agreement on wages and the other points, of which there were altogether about 12 in the memorandum. I may say that at that particular meeting there were no representatives of the Shipping Federation present. Those present were myself, my three cabinet colleagues, the mediator, the union representatives and their lawyer. Only five or six of the union representatives were present; the others were waiting outside.
After we had discussed this matter for the better part of an hour we adjourned to a room in the west block where simultaneous translating facilities are available so that those of the members who were in attendance who did not understand English would have the benefit of full discussion. During that meeting, which lasted nearly an hour, my

cabinet colleagues and I said we intended to meet that afternoon with the representatives of the Shipping Federation and that we would try to find out how far the Shipping Federation would go to improve the terms of payment contained in the counterproposal to which I referred, and which the Minister of Transport had in his hands, if they got a definite assurance from us that the findings of the commission of the crucial issues might be binding. I am not saying the word "crucial" was used, but I refer to the three or four outstanding points.
At that same meeting the president of the C.L.C. stated that he was leaving because of a prior engagement and would not be present at the meetings held later that day. He again stated that the congress, as a matter of principle, was definitely opposed to binding legislation in disputes between labour and management. I am not sure he used the words "in principle" but that was the gist of what he said.
My cabinet colleagues and Judge Lippe and I left that meeting, having conveyed to all the people present in English and through simultaneous translation, that we were going to put this proposal before the Shipping Federation together with the suggestion that, if the parties could agree on all the outstanding points except the three or four I mentioned, we were prepared to recommend that parliament make these findings binding.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
After lunch my three colleagues and Judge Lippe and I, met with the representatives of the Shipping Federation and their lawyer. We had a very full discussion. In fact, the discussion took so long that I thought that perhaps our persuasive powers had lost some of their effectiveness. In the meantime the longshoremen left the building after waiting two or three hours. They returned later. Nevertheless, even though the I.L.A. members had left, we continued our efforts and in the very late afternoon the Shipping Federation said that they were prepared to agree to a substantial wage increase and other benefits mentioned in the memorandum, subject to some details which had to be worked out as to whether it was 20 cents on return to work and 20 cents retroactive or some other terms. These were matters of detail.
There was discussion also about what the terms would be in 1967 and how they could be tied in with the findings of a commission of inquiry, if it were set up. However, in principle, they agreed to take their chances
July 14, 1966

with what an industrial inquiry commission might find in the field of increased productivity. If the commission found that the gang structure should be limited to 16 or 17 or 15 or should be increased to 19, which the Shipping Federation would not concede, they would accept these findings and would take their chances on them. They then agreed in return for that to give 40 cents per hour for 1966 and an additional 40 cents that was requested for 1967. There were some other items in the middle about which there did not seem to be any difficulty, as I have mentioned.
I might say that when the Shipping Federation agreed that they would meet the demands on wages within reason subject to the negotiation of certain details, my colleagues and I, with the knowledge and approval of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) because the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) who was Acting Prime Minister and I had both talked to him earlier in the morning, gave such an assurance. I might say that after a full month of a crippling strike, crippling not only to the people of Canada but to the workers and others directly involved, we felt as a government, or working as a committee of the government speaking for the government, that we had no alternative but to accept our responsibility as a government and to recommend legislation to parliament if the parties, as I have said, could agree to the wages and these other times. The Minister of Transport and I both made that quite clear to both sides.
After the Shipping Federation had agreed to this proposal, subject to negotiation of these details, my colleagues and I along with Judge Lippe met during the evening with the union representatives and their lawyer to discuss the proposal that had come out of our lengthy afternoon meeting with the Shipping Federation and our earlier morning meeting with the longshoremen. As I have mentioned, Mr. Jodoin was not there during the afternoon or evening meetings.
I want to say to this house in unequivocal terms that in my view, and in the opinion of those of my colleagues who were present during the final stages of these negotiations, there is not the slightest doubt but that the Shipping Federation would not have agreed to a settlement along lines, which some of the union members later referred to as fabulous, had we not made to them a clear and positive commitment of the nature to which I have referred.
Labour Conditions
I want to assure this house also that Mr. Cutler, the legal adviser, and the I.L.A. negotiators were aware of every step of the negotiations from approximately 11.30 in the morning of Saturday, June 11, and that if the parties could agree on wages and these other issues, we were prepared to recommend to parliament legislative action which would make the commission's findings binding with regard to gang structure, sling loads consistent with safety, job security of longshoremen in good standing and related matters. Our whole course of action-when I say "our" I refer to my three cabinet colleagues, the Minister of Transport, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Favreau) the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Mac-Eachen) and myself-on Saturday morning and early Sunday was predicated on the fact that the Shipping Federation and the Longshoremen's Association knew the course we had in mind, and that the later discussions that took place on wages and what the division would be between an allowance for job security and an allowance for straight wages were predicated on that knowledge. I might say again, in view of some of the newspaper articles that have appeared, that though the union representatives did not join in the request for a commission, nor did they formally agree to having the representations implemented by legislation, to say the least they appeared to be realistic. They wanted to see the matter settled and they wanted to see it settled as quickly as possible.
They led us to believe that, if agreement could be reached on the points mentioned by the Minister of Transport, they would cooperate with the commission and that they would obey any law that parliament might pass making these findings binding. I might say that even though the negotiations were broken off and we were tired and disappointed, I was still hopeful a settlement would be reached. It did not seem to me that there were too many differences. I was confirmed in that opinion when on Monday morning, June 13, while my three colleagues and I were in the Prime Minister's office, a telephone call came through to the Prime Minister. It was from Mr. Jodoin. The Prime Minister turned to us and said that Mr. Jodoin had said he was speaking on behalf of the I.L.A. and asked the Prime Minister if we would receive a representative group from the Longshoremen's Association. The Prime Minister, again relaying his conversation with Mr. Jodoin, told us what Mr. Jodoin had said to him-I

July 14, 1966
Labour Conditions
made a note of the words-that the parties were so close to an agreement the day before he thought a meeting with the Prime Minister present might bring an end to the dispute and result in an early return to work.
The Prime Minister suggested that if they were close to an agreement they might meet in the office of the Minister of Labour with me and the cabinet colleagues who I have mentioned. He gave an assurance the minister would try to get the representatives of the Shipping Federation to come to Ottawa for concurrent or subsequent discussions. As a result of that telephone call meetings did take place during the late afternoon and early evening of the 13th with representatives of the I.L.A. and representatives of the Shipping Federation. During the late evening of the 13th, from shortly before ten o'clock, and continuing into the early morning of the 14th, further meetings were held in the Prime Minister's office. I might say that the Prime Minister first met with representatives of the Shipping Federation but the I.L.A. representatives were in a room not far away. Then the Prime Minister, along with the rest of us, met with representatives of the I.L.A. Still later he met again with each of these groups separately, with the rest of us present.
Finally, the representatives of both parties met with us in the Prime Minister's office. By this time, nearly two o'clock in the morning, a settlement was reached. The settlement was announced to the press. Mr. Speaker, I think an incident occurred which is of very great importance. An aide-memoire had been prepared by my colleagues and myself for the Prime Minister's use. This aide-memoire is most important because it confirms definitely the fact that the findings of the commission on these limited issues were to be made binding by legislation.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I should like to read into the record the memorandum which the Prime Minister read, first to the representatives of the Shipping Federation:
At the meeting of the cabinet committee this afternoon with the bargaining committee of the
I.LA. there remained three points outstanding, as follows.
1.	Saturday call in.
2.	The application of retroactivity on overtime.
3.	Four hour recall.
I understand that the first item has been disposed of and I will not raise the matter at this point for consideration.
I propose to ask the I.L.A. to drop its demand for the application of retroactivity on overtime. I am now asking the representatives of the Shipping

Federation to accept the following proposal with respect to the four hour recall:
1.	That the four hour recall be instituted when, the men return to work.
2.	That this item-
The recall item.
-be submitted to the commission for examination, and that the recommendation of the commission with respect to this item be binding in precisely the same way as the recommendation with respect to gang size. The four hour recall would then be dealt with and included within the contract in the manner specified by the commission.
After that proposal had been placed by the Prime Minister before the Shipping Federation representatives they adjourned to caucus. Then the Prime Minister with the same persons present, the cabinet colleagues to whom I have referred and Judge Lippe, invited the representatives of the Shipping Federation into his office and he read them this statement, except that it was in the converse.

speechtext: I presume the minister means the I.L.A. representatives.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
I beg your pardon, yes, the I.L.A. I will skip the introductory part. Again the Prime Minister said:
I understand that the first item has been disposed of and I will not raise the matter at this point for consideration.
When speaking to the I.L.A. representatives he used these words:
I now ask you-
The I.L.A.
-to drop your demand for the application of retroactivity on overtime.
These are the notes that I made when this statement was being read with the representatives present. The Prime Minister continued:
I have asked the representatives of the Shipping Federation to accept the following proposal with respect to the four hour recall:
1.	That the four hour recall be instituted when the men return to work.
2.	That this item be submitted to the commission for examination, and that the recommendation of the commission with respect to this item be binding in precisely the same way as the recommendation with respect to gang size. The four hour recall would then be dealt with and included within the contract in the manner specified by the commission.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
May I ask the minister a question at this point? Am I right in thinking that at this meeting the president of the Canadian. Labour Congress was present?
July 14. 1966

Labour Conditions

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
At this meeting, Mr. Speaker, the president of the Canadian Labour Congress was present. I might say that he took relatively little part in the conversation at that time, although at one stage, again in fairness to him, he did say: "You know, Mr. Prime Minister, we are opposed to legislation which makes any findings of a commission binding", or words to that effect.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, agreement was reached on the strength of the assurance that we gave to the Shipping Federation. We gave it with prior knowledge on the part of the I.L.A. that we were going to discuss this. For approximately three or four hours, perhaps longer, late Saturday night, the 11th, and on the early morning of the 12th, we did not discuss in detail wages and some other items in the eight or nine other areas upon which basically agreement had been reached. But we did discuss whether the 40 cents payable in 1957, that is, the second part of it, would be payable when the commission report came in and whether it would be payable on April 1, May 1, or June 1. These points were discussed at some length.
Before we left the Prime Minister's office and after we had all been photographed, I might say that I saw many of the longshoremen officials shaking hands with some of the officials of the Shipping Federation, with whom they were hardly on speaking terms a month before when I first met them. It was a very jovial, happy occasion. Photographs were taken in which they, Mr. Jodoin and the rest of us participated. When we left the Prime Minister's office it was agreed that the lawyers for the two parties and certain other representatives, not all of them but enough to be truly representative, would meet in my office later the same morning to prepare minutes of settlement.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, as you already know, that the terms of settlement were filed in this chamber, along with certain other documents, by my parliamentary secretary on the 8th instant.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext: Would the minister forgive me if I ask another question at this point? Do I understand him to suggest that the first draft of the terms of settlement was prepared by the lawyers for the two parties and that a draft was not prepared by his department which was presented to them?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
I am glad that question has been asked. When the parties reassembled, knowing that time was an important factor
my deputy minister had taken it upon himself, he having been present throughout the whole proceedings, to draft what he thought might be minutes helpful to both sides, because he had no particular axe to grind one way or the other. This draft was then submitted to both sides. I was there for part of the discussion but not for all of it. Several changes were made in the draft which was prepared by my deputy minister, Dr. Hay-thorne.
One significant change which I remember very clearly was this. If you look at Hansard for July 8, page 7436, the 12 points on which agreement had been reached are enumerated there. Then appears this paragraph:
The agreements terminating on December 31, 1965, shall be amended by incorporating therein the terms of settlement set out above-
Those are the old agreements which expired last year.
-and these amended agreements-
The agreements amended by the terms of settlement to which I have referred.
-shall remain in effect until December 31, 1967, unless amended by negotiations-
Then I actually said: "What about the binding legislation? There is no reference to that and that has clearly been understood." Therefore, the words "or otherwise" which appear in the seventh last line on that page were inserted to cover that situation; there is not the slightest question about that. Mr. Cutler himself discussed the words with me, as did Mr. Pathy representing the I.L.A. Judge Lippe and my deputy minister were there and they took part in discussing whether better words might be used.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext: They were delightfully uninformative.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
I will tell you why, just to be clear on this for my hon. friend. The Longshoremen's Association had taken the position that they did not want to commit themselves to something that had binding legislation in it. But it was definitely understood that the words "or otherwise" covered that situation, and that was the purpose of putting them in. Whether it was done by agreement or by legislation, that covered it. The only other way you can change a binding agreement, except by agreement, is by legislation; there is not the slightest question about that. I am sure that if Mr. Cutler, Mr. Pathy or the others were questioned about this they would confirm that that was the situation.

July 14, 1966
Labour Conditions
When I announced the settlement in the house on the afternoon of that day, I said that an industrial commission would be established and that I would have more to say on that subject after the commission was established. It has since been suggested in this house by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) that I should have advised the house at that time that the government intended to introduce legislation along the lines of the present bill. I had a statement to this effect prepared. Originally such a statement was included in the notes that I subsequently used in the house.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
As a matter of courtesy and fair dealing I showed it to the legal adviser for the Longshoremen's Association. He said: "I hope, Mr. Minister, that you will not have to refer to binding legislation when speaking in the house because, acting for the longshoremen, my clients should have an opportunity to explain the settlement to their members and they might get a mistaken idea if you make reference to the legislation aspect in the house." I amended the notes accordingly, and I believe that the paper that went to the Hansard office will show that. That seemed to be a reasonable request from Mr. Cutler, and I complied with it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext: Before the minister leaves that point, may I ask him whether the same considerations applied when the minister was making the announcement of the commission itself?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
I think that all I did at that time was to table the document, knowing that I expected to introduce the bill within a day or two. I just tabled the document and, as I recall, made no statement.
It is the considered view of the government that the passage of this legislation at this time is both advisable and necessary in order to fulfil the undertaking which we, with the knowledge though perhaps not with the actual consent of the unions, gave to the federation.
The new pay rates provided for in this agreement, namely, the extra 40 cents an hour and the retroactive features, are now in effect. I can assure members of the house, if they need any further assurance, that there would have been no settlement without such an undertaking and there would have been no return to work. We were prepared to leave the matter in the hands of parliament,
(Mr. Nicholson.]
with a strong recommendation to be made in the light of the history I have recited.
The government believes that its commitment should be fulfilled at this time and not later. It should be done now when the matter is fresh in the minds of those who participated in the final discussions. It should not be done some months from now.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to a letter which I received from Mr. Cutler, whom I met frequently in the course of these negotiations. I found Mr. Cutler co-operative. He wrote me a letter dated June 20 which is of some significance because it includes the legal opinion he had given to his clients, which opinion was addressed to Mr. Tremblay, vice president of the International Longshoremen's Association.
When I received that letter I wrote the letter to Mr. Cutler appearing on page 7438 of Hansard. I shall read that:
Dear Mr. Cutler:
I received your letter of June 20 and appreciate your action in forwarding a copy of your letter of June 16 to Mr. Gerard Tremblay, Vice President of the Atlantic coast district of the International Longshoremen's Association.
In order to clear up any possible misunderstanding with respect to the settlement reached on June 14 between the International Longshoremen's Association locals in Montreal, Trois-Rivi&res and Quebec and The Shipping Federation of Canada, there are a few observations which I would like to make on your letter to Mr. Tremblay.
During our discussions on June 13 and 14 and previously on June 11 and 12, both Mr. Pickersgill, who was the Acting Prime Minister in Mr. Pearson's absence over the week end, and I stated that, provided the parties reached agreement on all of the other items in dispute, the government was prepared to establish an industrial inquiry commission to carry out an independent and objective study of problems in connection with improvements in productivity, job security and related matters, and to take steps to have the conclusions reached as a result of this independent industiral inquiry commission implemented by legislative enactment.
You will recall that the same commitment was made by the Prime Minister during the meetings held in his office on the night of June 13.
This commitment was directly associated throughout our discussions with the wage settlement for both 1966 and 1967 which, as you know, was only accepted by The Shipping Federation of Canada on the strength of this commitment.
I do not think I need read the rest of the letter.
After that letter was written I received a message from Mr. Cutler suggesting that the terms of reference of the industrial inquiry commission which I had filed in the house were not clear enough, that provision had not been made for job security for some people who may have worked less than enough time
July 14, 1966

Labour Conditions
to give them certain sick benefits that are referred to under the collective agreement. Mr. Cutler, I think properly, complained to me and to my department that the terms were ambiguous and should be cleared up.
I said: "If there is any ambiguity about them, they will be cleared up, because I told you positively that the terms would include job security for all bona fide union longshoremen, whether they have worked 300 hours or 1,000 hours." I recall that I used the expression to him that people with arthritic backs might come to work for three or four hours a day or for three shifts a week. I said that we were prepared to leave problems such as these to the industrial inquiry commissioner to decide, and that if there was any doubt about the terms of the commission we would clarify them. When I spoke to Mr. Cutler on the telephone he said that he had received the letter and that there was no misunderstanding with regard to its contents.
On June 30 the Prime Minister and I received telegrams, copies of which appear on pages 7439 and 7440 of Hansard. I do not need to refer to those telegrams in detail because they can be found in that part of Hansard to which reference has already been made. In this connection I wish to direct hon. members' attention to pages 7440 and 7441 of Hansard. I repeated exactly the same thing in those telegrams.
The Prime Minister sent a telegram shortly after I did saying he was familiar with the contents of my telegram and referring to this memorandum that I have read out today. I shall read the Prime Minister's words, and I quote from page 7442 of Hansard:
Referring your telegram to me of today's date in which you refer to your wire to Minister of Labour I have seen his telegram in reply. My own knowledge of the facts fully confirms this reply.
This refers to the statement that finally the matter would be made binding by legislation which was read to the longshoremen or their lawyers in Mr. Jodoin's presence late on the night of June 13 and the early morning of June 14.
The bill now before the house, Mr. Speaker, is short. It speaks for itself. On behalf of the government and in light of the facts as I have related them, I would ask for its early passage.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) in his concluding remarks said that the commitment should be fulfilled. The obvious question arising in one's mind is, to whom? I shall have something to say about that later.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I must confess I felt somewhat sorry for the Minister of Labour because he has had to relive the events he has spoken of. He had to tread that tortuous path of events again not only on Monday last but also today for almost two hours. I also felt sorry for him as he wound his way through the gamut of discussions, meetings, luncheons and dinners. The disappointing part is that he eventually came to a point of inconclusion because in presenting this bill he admits that all the matters in dispute between the shipping companies and the I.L.A. were not dealt with. Today we are being asked to deal with Bill C-215 to complete the dealings between the two parties to the dispute, the shipping companies and the I.L.A.
There are two parts to the preamble to the bill and the first paragraph contains the following:
-it was recommended that an industrial inquiry commission be appointed under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act to inquire into certain matters on which agreement was not reached and to report its conclusions thereon to the Minister of Labour at the earliest possible date;
I can agree with that. In fact, no one in the house would be in disagreement with it. But the second part of the preamble reads:
And whereas an industrial inquiry commission to inquire into those certain matters has been appointed under the said act, and it is in the national interest that the conclusions of the said commission with respect thereto be carried into effect without delay following receipt of the report of the said commission, by the incorporation of those conclusions in the terms of settlement that were entered into following the settlement of the other issues involved in the dispute and in any collective agreements entered into pursuant to those terms of settlement:
The second part of the preamble is nothing else but compulsory arbitration, and compulsory arbitration in its most extreme form. Not only are the terms binding on both parties but they are to be imposed before knowing what they are. Today parliament is being asked to impose upon labour and management conditions which have not yet been decided upon or revealed.
I ask myself, what has happened to this government, a government which until recently on every occasion hid its activity in respect of this matter behind the curtain of the principle of free collective bargaining? I am not going to set out the events as my colleague from Halifax will do that, but when the government was asked questions time and again during the question period respecting

July 14. 1966
Labour Conditions
the progress of the dispute and the activity of the Minister of Labour, it maintained that it believed in the principle of free collective bargaining. Yet today we are being asked to pass a bill to impose the conclusions of a commission of inquiry upon labour and management, and make those conditions part of a collective agreement even before they have been reached. In my opinion this represents a total breakdown of the machinery of collective bargaining.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
In its defence the government says that this is necessary, but I say to the government that no legislation is necessary at this point at all. A commissioner can be appointed. No one will object to that. The commissioner can go to work and eventually, upon hearing both sides and investigating the situation completely, he can make a report to the Minister of Labour who in turn should refer that report to the interested parties as a basis for collective bargaining.
Today the government is not following the collective bargaining procedure. It has abandoned the principle which it led us to believe it believed in. It has thrown that principle to the winds. Members of the government are saying that compulsory arbitration is now the order of the day in the settlement of disputes between management and labour. They are -saying: This is what we want; we do not know what the recommendations will be but we want them rubberstamped before they are made and parliament will be that rubber stamp.
This legislation is based on assumption. The government is assuming that the recommendations will be acceptable to both parties. What will be the situation if the recommendations are not acceptable? Will that tend to a happy and harmonious situation between these two parties for the duration of the present agreement? This is almost prophetic legislation. We do not know what is going to be recommended but we are being asked to put unknown recommendations into effect.
I say that this approach makes a mockery out of parliament. It makes a mockery out of [DOT]collective bargaining. What remedy would there be if an error were made in the recommendations? If this legislation is passed and a report is made to the minister, it then becomes law. How can it be changed? It will be fixed and unalterable and will require action by parliament to make even the slightest alteration, however beneficial it might be.
tMr. Starr.]
This is the kind of thing a government resorts to when it cannot cope with a situation, and this government has proven to be inept, indecisive and incompetent in matters of this kind. It has allowed such matters to drag on day after day, week after week, month after month, in this particular case for over a month, before acting, and it acted only when the tie-up of the ports was in danger of bringing about an economic crisis. Then and only then did the government proceed by way of concessions to both sides.
How did the government get management to accept the increased wage packet? I would say obviously by giving an assurance that an inquiry would be set up and that binding recommendations would be imposed regarding the work gangs and the loading and unloading operations. In fact, the Minister of Labour admits this. In this connection I quote from the remarks he made on Monday, July 11, as recorded at page 7523 of Hansard. They are interesting because I think this is the crux of the whole situation. He said:
We left the morning meeting at about 1.30 p.m. to meet with the Shipping Federation with whom we spent several hours in the afternoon. They insisted-
The Shipping Federation.
-that an agreement must be reached for the reorganization of longshoremen's gangs, new types of slings and other changes that might result in increased productivity. Eventually they did agree that if the government would take the responsibility for setting up the commission and agree to pass legislation, they would acquiesce in such a course and would agree to the second payment of 40 cents in 1967; 15 cents were paid on January 1 and 25 cents later in the year when the recommendations of the commission were implemented.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
This was the deal; this was the basis upon which this government then proceeded. What was the reaction? The Minister of Labour in his statement the other day said the reaction was not one of acceptance. He said that the unions then stated they could not go along with the proposal for this commission. If the government wishes to establish the commission it can. They have no power to stop the government setting up a commission. In his statement on Monday last, at page 7523 of Hansard, the minister said:
There were further discussions in the afternoon during which there was no doubt as to their acquiescence to certain aspects of the proposal.
What aspects of the proposal?
-the president of the Canadian Labour Congress said again that the Congress was opposed to compulsory arbitration and that he wanted to make it clear.
July 14, 1966

Mr. Cutler, according to the Minister of Labour, said that if the government does set up a commission and if the government is prepared to take the responsibility of making findings, "we will obey the law". Why not? The representatives of Canadian unions certainly obey the law. What else can they do if this government forces compulsory arbitration? If it becomes law the members of the union, who are good Canadians, will obey the law. That does not mean they acquiesce in the procedure now being taken by this House of Commons.
I say that all the statements which have been cited by the Minister of Labour as having been made by the president of the Canadian Labour Congress and the representatives of the I.L.A. are emphatic statements of opposition to compulsory arbitration. In view of these emphatic statements, was it not obvious at that time and is it not obvious now to the government that compulsory arbitration was not and is not acceptable? Yet the government goes ahead because of a commitment to the shipping companies. Why is parliament today asked to impose compulsory arbitration and buy a pig in a poke, to use the words of the Minister of Labour?
We of this party always have been against compulsory arbitration and in this particular instance we will oppose this legislation and vote against it. This is a last resort against the will of the unions who want to protect collective bargaining. This matter can be settled under the collective bargaining procedure. This is a serious mistake. I should like to repeat what I said earlier. The commission should be set up and the commissioner should make his inquiry. He should make his recommendations and the Minister of Labour could then take the recommendations and submit them to the parties. Then the two parties could study the report in an effort to ascertain whether or not it provided a basis for agreement.
As I said, under those circumstances there was no need for this legislation. This bill sets a very dangerous precedent. It says to management and to labour: This is it; we, the government, will legislate for you regardless of your wishes because we know best how these matters can be settled. This matter should be dealt with when the contents of the report are known and the recommendations have been made public and not before.
I say to the minister and to the government that this matter should be reconsidered. The
Labour Conditions
government should not jeopardize the position of free collective bargaining, something which they have said they stand for. Now they have thrown it overboard. They should reconsider their position. A commission should be established, a report made, that report should then be the basis for collective bargaining between the two parties much in the way a conciliation board report is. There should be an opportunity for free collective bargaining and not compulsory arbitration regardless of what the recommendations are.
What if the recommendations are not agreeable to the Minister of Labour himself? What if they are contrary to the things we stand for? How can you impose upon management and labour the conditions in a report? They might not agree and would have to pay for it for the balance of the life of the agreement. I say to the government that they are doing a very dangerous thing in introducing this bill. They are setting a bad precedent. They ought to reconsider this matter and withdraw the bill. They should set up a commission which would make its recommendations and submit them to the two parties as a basis for collective bargaining procedure.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to begin my remarks on this occasion by expressing my appreciation of the very clear and able presentation of the case which the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) has made. I suggest to the minister that the hon. member for Ontario placed the case before him in a reasoned and restrained way, as I too hope to try to do. I should like to join him in his request that the minister and the government reconsider their insistence on this legislation being placed before us.
I appreciate fully the difficulties which the minister had in this very important struggle on the waterfronts of Montreal, Quebec and Trois-Rivieres. I do so because, as hon. members know, I have had many years experience in a professional capacity in labour relations. Indeed, I have acted for many unions in Ontario and throughout Canada. I have acted also for locals of the International Longshoremen's Association in Toronto and Hamilton. I have had no dealings with locals in the province of Quebec but I have acted, as I said, for Ontario locals.
Therefore I appreciate fully that the parties are perhaps not the most flexible in labour negotiations. I can understand that on many occasions during the many weeks of

July 14, 1966
Labour Conditions
strike the minister and his colleagues, like all of us in this house, felt rather desperate about the developing situation. I say to him, however, that the bill he has proposed is totally unjustified. It is an evil yielding to the pressure of one side in the dispute. It is giving in to the Shipping Federation which is a rather tough outfit. It is legislation forced on the government by the Shipping Federation, and if it is legislation which the government really supports in principle, then this government stands condemned in the annals of labour history in this country.
I say to the minister that the legislation is wrong in principle. I say to him that it perverts the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act under which he appointed the commissioner of inquiry. I say to him it is also recklessly premature. It is an indication of weakness on the part of the minister and the government and is a shameful abdication of their responsibility to the labour movement of Canada.
Throughout his feeble defence of this bill the minister has been trying to place the responsibility for it in part on his contention that the union, if it did not actually agree, may have acquiesced and that if it did not actually acquiesce it at least knew it was coming. I say to him that in spite of his words, and I am not for one moment questioning his veracity or honesty, the record, as contained in the documents which he filed and which are appended to Hansard of Friday, July 8, 1966, shows that the union categorically denies any approval of binding arbitration and has insisted that the minister cannot use the pretence that the union approved as a defence for his action. That fact is stated in the letter which the minister quoted from Mr. Cutler to Mr. Tremblay. It was also stated in the telegrams which have been tabled and form part of the appendix. I do not wish to take the time to read them; they are on record. I challenge the minister to show me in any communication from Mr. Cutler to him or to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) that has been tabled or appended to Hansard one word of acquiescence or agreement to binding arbitration legislation.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I continually asked the minister to table these documents, but I must say I got fed up asking. There is another document in the minister's possession which he ought to have tabled. I refer to the telegram from the president of the Canadian Labour Congress, Mr. Claude Jodoin, dated July 8, 1966 to the

minister, a copy of which Mr. Jodoin sent me. The telegram reads as follows:
Following telegram sent today to labour minister Nicholson quote answer your telegram July 7, at no time was there any agreement by the I.L.A. in my presence nor by myself on behalf of the C.L.C. to compulsory or binding arbitration. I regret to have to disagree with your account of the discussions. References to an inquiry were to an investigation which would look into the situation with a view to possibly making suggestions which might be considered by the parties. It was the position of I.L.A. that such consideration would have to take place in the next negotiations. If compulsory legislation is introduced it will clearly be the responsibility of the government and in no sense can be attributed to any agreement made by the union.
Claude Jodoin President C.L.C.
Any one of us who have had any experience in labour negotiations-

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit me to ask him a question for the purpose of clarification? Is it not correct that he received that telegram after the documents were tabled on July 8? I am sure he does not want to leave the impression that the minister deliberately did not table that document. A copy of it was sent to me and it reached me well after the other documents were tabled.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext: The Minister of Transport is quite right. I received it after the documents were tabled. I am not accusing the Minister of Labour of hiding anything. But several days have passed since July 8 on any one of which he could have tabled this document. Surely it is not necessary, in respect of such an important matter, for us on this side of the house to keep pulling documents from him one by one. I was on the verge of asking him to table it on several occasions but I said to myself: No, I will wait and read it into the record. The document was in his hands and he could have tabled it at some time since July 8. I became fed up trying to get these documents tabled.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Did you not succeed in having a whole batch of documents tabled on just one occasion shortly after your request? You did not get them one by one.
