speechtext:
If the minister wants to go into this subject, let me remind him that I asked him for correspondence between the union and himself, between the union and the Prime Minister and between the congress and the minister. I then asked him whether he would table the aide-memoire to which he
July 14, 1966

referred today. I asked for this correspondence on several occasions, in fact, so often that I reached the end of my tether.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext: Will the hon. member not agree that within two minutes of the time of his request I tabled all the correspondence which now appears as an appendix to Hansard.1?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDING OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
I have no intention of attacking the integrity of the minister. He did file this correspondence, but in doing so he failed in a minor way in his duty in not tabling the telegram from Mr. Jodoin. I merely point that out, and that is as far as I wish to go.
In any case I suggest to the minister that in spite of his explanation I, as one member of many in this house, was misled by him, inadvertently no doubt, as to what his intentions were. At no time until he actually introduced this bill did he suggest what was in his mind with regard to compulsory arbitration.
Let me refer to the statement of the Prime Minister made on June 9 in answer to a question asked by my leader, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas). This is recorded in Hansard for that date at page 6173. The Prime Minister said:
Contrary to what the hon. member has suggested, and to what was suggested in the press release I have received from the New Democratic Party to the effect that there is no hope of an early breakthrough, there is hope of success in the negotiations.
We have not given up that hope. Judge Lippe is negotiating at this moment; we have been in touch with him during the last hour and we have not by any means given up hope that this serious issue will be settled very shortly by the processes of free collective bargaining and not by parliamentary direction.
If one reads the minister's statement of June 14 he will see that the minister made no reference to what Judge Lippe said or what Mr. Cutler suggested. His statement made it quite clear that the commissioner of inquiry to be appointed was to be appointed under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. If my memory serves me correctly, he used those very words. One does not have to be a labour expert to know that a commissioner appointed under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act does not make binding recommendations but that he makes recommendations for the parties to consider.
When the minister appointed a commissioner under the provisions of that act, whether he intended it or not he misled this house and
Labour Conditions
the labour movement. He may not have intended to do that, but the objective result was that he misled all of us as to what this commissioner of inquiry would do.
When the minister tabled the document appointing the commissioner on June 23-this is to be found on page 6785 of Hansard-he made a short statement to the effect that he was tabling the document appointing the commissioner. He could have indicated his intention, at that time, but he did not.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I apparently have mislaid the order in council appointing the commissioner but I venture to rely on my memory and state that the preamble to the appointment referred to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, indicating clearly that the commissioner of inquiry was being appointed pursuant to that act. I repeat again that any commissioner appointed pursuant to that act is a person who makes recommendations for the consideration of the parties, and he is not a final and binding arbitrator. Nor, I suggest to the minister, can he hang this legislation around Judge Lippe's neck. I appreciate that in his presentation today the minister seemed to suggest-I did not hear exactly what he said-that verbally Judge Lippe suggested that the findings of the commission be final and binding. But it is a most interesting coincidence that the date of Judge Lippe's report, which was tabled, is June 23, 1966, precisely the date on which the minister appointed the commissioner of inquiry under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act without saying anything about making his conclusions final and binding.
What has happened in this case, I suggest to the minister with the greatest respect, is that two things were being presented by the government and by Judge Lippe and, whether deliberately or otherwise, the two things have been scrambled in their presentation to this house. One, an entirely separate thing that was presented to the parties and was discussed, was the appointment of a commission of inquiry under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act for the purpose of inquiring into the question of productivity and making recommendations thereon. Everybody on both sides of the quarrel knew that this was not a mandatory thing, that the recommendations are not obligatory, not compulsory, but that on the contrary they are voluntarily put before the parties for their consideration.

July 14, 1966
Labour Conditions
Later in the game the Shipping Federation apparently said, "We will not give any increase in the second year unless we have this improvement in productivity and therefore you must tell us that you will make mandatory the results of the commissioner's findings. Otherwise we will not play the game." The minister and the government said, "O.K., boys; if that is your wish we will do it for you."
That undertaking, that promise to the Shipping Federation, need not necessarily have anything to do with the appointment of a commissioner of inquiry. Time and time again the minister in his statement said, "The union said they would co-operate with a commissioner of inquiry." Of course they would. Why wouldn't they? The fact is that they refused at first but finally they said, "All right, we will co-operate." Indeed, you cannot have a commission of inquiry looking into anything unless the union co-operates; otherwise the commission of inquiry is not worth a hoot in hades. You cannot have a commission of inquiry looking into the size of gangs and what the union members do unless the union is there, brings witnesses and presents its case. Until such time as you get the union to co-operate, the appointment of a commissioner is, of course, an entirely useless act. So they were finally persuaded to co-operate with the commissioner.
Time and time again-I repeat this because it is important-whether deliberately or not the minister scrambles up the perfectly sensible appointment of a commissioner of inquiry to give the facts to the parties, in order that they may be able to discuss what they want to do about them, with the second fact which is entirely unrelated to it, namely, making the commissioner a compulsory arbitrator. And the minister places in the mouth of the union spokesman statements-I say this without intending any offence to him although perhaps I should not be so kind in view of the legislation that has been put before us -relating to the appointing of a commissioner and to binding arbitration as if they were both made in one sentence at the same time. He knows very well they were not. He knows very well that the reply to one had an entirely different context from the reply to the other.

May I summarize my reasons for moving this amendment. The first reason, to which I have not yet alluded, is that I am sorry to have to inform the Minister of Labour that I have had long conversations with Mr. Cutler, whom I have known for many years, and I have had some conversations with Mr. Jo-doin, and those gentlemen, with whom I have taken up the precise statements made by the minister in this house, do not recall what transpired in precisely the same way as the minister does. Mr. Speaker, I think we must maintain the principle. Binding arbitration has existed and still exists. It is not an absolute principle. It is not a principle which cannot be waived; the parties themselves waive it in many circumstances.
In collective agreements, there may be arbitration not only on the interpretation and violation of the collective agreement, but also on conflicts of interests which can occur during the collective agreement. That exists. The parties' will is then respected. Binding arbitration exists by virtue of our provincial and even our federal legislation. Under the federal legislation on industrial relations, collective agreements must contain a clause providing for the settlement of grievances compulsorily or by an arbitration during the collective agreement. If insurance is being offered for fire protection and no other companies are providing coverage, then obviously there would be merit in the establishment of an insurance company that would do this. But I believe that literally thousands and thousands of companies issue fire insurance. I think it should be ascertained whether or not it is proper to expand the number of such companies. I can see one obvious reason companies are formed and why they should be issuing certain types of insurance, but in my opinion one of the roles of the Superintendent of Insurance is to indicate whether or not there is a need, room or place for another company. This should be true when Aetna Casualty Company of Canada makes this application.

-and we are really submitting more to the jurisdiction rather than less in asking the committee to approve the incorporation of a Canadian company. Mr. Chairman, one of the basic things we must consider, not only in respect of this bill but in respect of all insurance companies seeking incorporation in bills now before us, is the degree to which the companies are owned or effectively controlled in Canada. In other words, are these companies Canadian or subsidiaries of foreign companies? I understand that in the case of the Aetna Casualty Company it is a wholly owned subsidiary of a United States company, the name of which escapes me for the moment. If I am incorrect in this regard I am sure the sponsor of the bill will correct me. I have just been informed that the parent of this company has its head office in Hartford, Connecticut, so I am right in my thinking.
Since 1962, when the Liberal party decided to develop policies in respect of foreign control of service industries in Canada, we have come to accept the idea that the Liberals believe in Canadian ownership. The former minister of finance spoke at that time as he does now in favour of the concept of Canadian control rather than control resting
Private Bills
in the hands of foreigners who are not answerable to Canadian laws for the activities of their subsidiary companies. That hon. member still holds a great deal of influence in the ranks of the Liberal party. However, what has happened in respect of the Bank Act may prove me wrong in that connection. I usually refer to the former minister of finance, but I understand that hon. member who represents Davenport still receives a considerable degree of support for his enunciated ideas. Other Liberals support the idea of Canadian ownership of industries in Canada.
At some subsequent stage of the proceedings in respect of the bill now before us I intend to move certain appropriate amendments in order to ensure that in respect of this company there is the desired Canadian ownership, authority and control. One of the amendments I intend to move, and it could be moved in regard to the clause we are now considering, will be such as to require that all the directors of applicant companies such as this be Canadian citizens ordinarily resident in Canada.
At the present time I understand that under the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act the majority of directors are required to be Canadian citizens. In this regard I should like to quote from the minutes and proceedings of June 14 of the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs. Mr. Humphrys, who is the Superintendent of the Department of Insurance, gave evidence on this question in reply to a question posed by the chairman. In reference to the application of the law in respect of Aetna he said at page 560:
As matters stand under the law, a United States company or a company from any country outside Canada, if it is in a strong financial condition can enter Canada and become registered under the Foreign Insurance Companies Act and transact insurance in Canada. Most countries offer reciprocal facilities to Canadian companies; they may enter foreign countries and transact business there. Where a company operates in Canada through a branch office such as the Aetna Casualty and Surety Company does now, the main direction of the company is, of course, at the home office of the company where the directors are situated and where the management is.
In other words, as Mr. Humphrys put it, the main direction of this company is in Hartford, Connecticut, and not at any place in Canada. He then stated:
The same thing applies when a Canadian company does business in the United States through a branch.

July 14. 1966

There is no argument about that fact, because it is a fact of economic life. Mr. Humphrys then stated:
But where foreign interests who want to do business in Canada incorporate a Canadian company, this requires a substantially larger Canadian content and a more extensive submission to Canadian laws and Canadian decisions than is the case of a branch.
I think there is some conflict in that attitude because, as I read Mr. Humphrys comments, when a company operates through a branch office the requirements of the law are not quite as stringent as they are if the company is incorporated in Canada under our procedures. It seems to me there should be an equitable application of the law, whatever it may be, to all companies whether they operate in Canada as incorporated companies or as subsidiaries. Then Mr. Humphrys made this point about directors of a Canadian company being Canadians. He said:
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
The requirement that a majority of the directors of a Canadian company be at all times Canadian citizens resident in Canada has been in our insurance laws for some years.
He is referring to the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act. Then he said:
For this company the law will require that a majority of the directors of this Canadian company at all times be Canadian citizens resident in Canada. This will represent a substantial step forward in the degree of Canadian control and Canadian decisions on the policies of this company.
In Mr. Humphrys' view this is a beneficial thing so far as Canada is concerned because, as he pointed out, when a company incorporates in this country the requirements are tougher than they are if they are just operating a branch office. Mr. Humphrys went on to say:
If a Canadian company were doing business in the United States and wished to incorporate a subsidiary there are no restrictions, of which I am aware, that would require all the directors of that subsidiary to be United States citizens. It would be customary and usual that the parent company would have some representation on the board of directors.
He was making the point that this is a step in the right direction and is a progressive move because it brings a larger degree of Canadian decision-making into the operation of the company. It seems logical to me, if the majority of the directors are required to be Canadian, that this in itself would bring about a larger degree of concern on the part of the company for Canadian interests. If the requirement were that all the directors be Canadian, we would be one more step ahead of the present situation.

Parliament has enacted such legislation before. A few years ago we made the requirement in respect of a pipe line company, the name of which I have forgotten, that all the directors be at all times Canadian citizens ordinarily resident in this country. It seems to me this is what we should be doing now, namely, thinking in terms of giving the fullest possible degree of Canadian control to these companies. We are on the verge of perhaps developing a different concept of the structure, management and operation of insurance companies. Perhaps between now and the time these matters are considered again we may be able to develop some well laid plans and ideas about the amendments that would be necessary to put into effect certain basic ideas that we have. One of these is that all the directors of the company shall at all times be Canadian citizens ordinarily resident' in Canada.
I do not intend to move an amendment at this moment, Mr. Chairman. Such an amendment could well fit into clause 1 because certain people are named therein, and it could also fit into clause 2. Perhaps it would more appropriately be made under clause 2. Mr. Humphrys referred to the requirement that the majority of the directors of a Canadian company be at all times Canadian citizens resident in this country and said it has been in our insurance laws for some years. I do not know how long this requirement has been in our insurance laws but it seems to me that if it has been there for some years we must consider the situation as it existed at the time the change was made and take into account the fact that there is today a far greater desire on the part of the Canadian people to have a greater degree of control over their industries than was the case some years ago.
The reason for Canadian people thinking this way is partly due to the farsighted opinions expressed by the former minister of finance. For this he deserves a great deal of credit. The former minister of finance expressed such opinions before his Prime Minister caught up with him, found that he was advancing ideas dangerous to the rightwing swing within the Liberal party and consequently eased him out of the cabinet. But the former minister of finance is directly responsible for there having developed in Canada a greater desire for an appreciation of the necessity of having Canadian control of our industry. In fact, one of his campaign slogans was "Buy Canada Back". These views of the former minister were widely circulated
July 14, 1966

in Weekend magazine or Star Weekly magazine through an extensive and well thought-out article which he wrote. Other writings of the former minister of finance have contributed to our people having this desire for greater Canadianism.
I believe we should be taking steps to reflect this desire in the laws we enact and this company should not be excluded. In saying this I am liable to be accused of picking and choosing and it may be said: Why should Aetna Casualty Company of Canada be treated differently from any other insurance company? This is a valid argument. Indeed, why should it be treated differently? It may be said that every other insurance company in Canada can go about its business with only the majority of its directors having to be Canadian, and why should we suddenly step into the picture and say that the situation with regard to this company is different and all its directors must be Canadian citizens?
It may also be argued: Why should we insist upon this requirement in respect of the Aetna company and not apply it to all the other insurance companies in respect of which bills appear on our order paper? I admit the validity of this argument but I believe we have to start somewhere. Perhaps we could start with at least a discussion of this very vital principle and we might then be able to persuade the government to introduce legislation to amend the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act and make this provision applicable to all insurance companies in Canada.
All I desire to do in this instance, Mr. Chairman, is make a start and follow along from Mr. Humphry's contention that this represents a forward step in the development of Canadian based decision-making. The hon. member for Sainte-Marie asked Mr. Humphrys questions in this respect, as reported at page 560 of the minutes of the proceedings of the committee:
When we talk. Mr. Humphrys, of management or directors, are we talking about any special responsibility in the conduct of the policy of the company itself or do these directors have no power at all to decide the policy of the company?
Mr. Humphrys replied as follows:
The board of directors is the highest management group in the company-
That is understandable.
-so the policy of the company would be established by the board of directors.

The hon. member for Sainte-Marie then said:
I am asking this question particularly because we do not know that policies may be drafted in the United States by the parent company and applied to the subsidiary here in Canada without any change at all in the application of the policy. This is where I am concerned.
And well might he be concerned. Mr. Humphrys answered in this way:
This is possible, sir, but I believe that formation of a separate Canadian company with its management and its business directed primarily toward the Canadian market, it is more likely to result in management policies and general business practices that are designed for the Canadian market to a greater extent than would be the case if the company continued to operate a branch office here.
I would say that so far as our department is concerned, we do not attempt to influence insurers either way, either through a branch office or through a subsidiary company but I do believe that the formation of a subsidiary company creates a stronger element of Canadian control and Canadian design in the insurance product than is the case where the operation is through a branch.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
I submit that this is an admission of failure, not on the part of Mr. Humphrys because he is only putting policy into effect but on the part of the government, to recognize the difference between the manner in which the requirements of the law are observed in so far as branch offices are concerned and those in regard to incorporated companies. It would seem to me, and I made this point earlier, that what the government should be doing is to make the law applicable universally so that it would apply to branch offices in the same manner as it does to Canadian companies. I do not know how this can be done but it will certainly require some alteration of the legislation because presumably there is no law requiring branch offices to have any degree of Canadian content or control; otherwise this requirement would be in effect. I simply leave it to those who have the responsibility of drafting the government's legislation to draw it up in such a manner that the law will apply equally to the two types of insurance operations.
Then Mr. Irvine followed this by saying-I do not know who Mr. Irvine is but presumably he is in some way connected with the company; maybe he is a member but I have never run across his name before:
The statement given under the preamble was a little technical which made it a little difficult for a person such as myself to understand it completely. This, as I understand it, is to be a Canadian company, a subsidiary of Aetna of Hartford operating in Canada and handling casualty only. Is this right?

speechtext:
In entering this debate, Mr. Chairman, first of all I want to lay some stress on the whole question of the insurance business. I have been somewhat concerned for quite some time about the proliferation of insurance companies of various types, and I think in the case of an insurance company of this nature it might be as well if we were first of all to define quite clearly just what sort of an operation we are dealing with because I have noticed that any operation which involves a financial institution invariably assumes in our society some air of respectability, almost of untouchability, and perhaps obscures the reality behind the facade. Obviously insurance companies of this sort are engaged in what could be termed a gambling business. We all gamble with our fire insurance companies that we will not have a fire and they gamble with us on that basis. I am not suggesting it is an illegal or immoral business but I am suggesting it is not necessarily an operation that is highly respectable because it is a financial one. It is a gambling proposition, and this company is asking us to allow them to engage in gambling in 26 various fields of possible accident, danger or loss.
My feeling on this point, Mr. Chairman, is that we have had an experience in one part of this country of a very satisfactory solution to the provision of gambling opportunities, if you like, in a certain type of accident which may occur to citizens, and that is in the field Of auto insurance. I suppose everyone knows that one province in Canada has established a gambling operation, if you like, against car

accidents which is conducted by the provincial government. The result is that the fortunate inhabitants of that province are able to protect themselves from automobile accidents at a fraction of the cost which those of us who live in other provinces must pay.
On that score I would suggest it is about time that we considered this whole proposition of protection from accidents on the same basis as the Saskatchewan car insurance operation which is still being continued under a Liberal government although it was established under a C.C.F. government. I think we should look very carefully at these insurance bills, even the ones that are not concerned with life insurance which provide even more matters to be examined than the casualty insurance companies. I will not deal with those matters because life insurance is not included here.
One of the points I want to stress, as my colleague from Skeena did, and perhaps pursue a little further is the question of a company which is entirely foreign owned moving into the gambling industry to extract from Canadian citizens a very handsome volume of premiums, I presume, or they would not be asking to be allowed to operate here.
Quite seriously, Mr. Chairman, this is a matter which should be causing great concern to Canadians on account of the effects of foreign ownership particularly of financial institutions. It is not only the former minister of finance who has expressed his concern about foreign ownership of financial institutions. His policy is being continued in one very important area by the present Minister of Finance. I suggest that if we are going to permit this type of operation, if we are going to permit foreign insurance companies to operate in Canada, we are going to add to one of the most serious problems of every Canadian government, and that is the question of the balance of payments. Admittedly the profits of this company which will be remitted to the U.S. will not in themselves have any great effect on the balance of payments, but I suggest to you, sir, that the gradual remission of interest and dividends by U.S. owned insurance companies plays a very important part in creating our balance of payments problem. For that reason I think it is of dubious value that we should allow still another such company to enter the field to draw from the available pool of Canadian earnings that go into this sort of protection and at the same time create more problems
July 14, 1966

lor our government which must eventually be dealt with.
I also think, Mr. Chairman, it is time we began to look at the insurance business from the point ol view of the traditional free enterprise competitive theory. We are often told, of course, that competition is the life of the economy, that competition is what provides us with cheap services and goods. It may be true in some instances but I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that it is not and cannot be true in the field of insurance of any sort.
I do not have before me the proceedings of the committee which unfortunately I was not able to attend, having been away at the time, so I am not sure what is the exact volume of business which this company conducts. I am not sure whether any figures were given to the committee with regard to the operational costs of this company. However, if they are similar to the costs of a company sponsored under another bill by the same hon. member and considered by the committee the other day, then I suggest to you, sir, that we have ample evidence that the proliferation of insurance companies of any type does not lead to cheaper and better service and lower premiums but must inevitably lead to the contrary. As I recall, in this other instance there were some 400 employees who were employed in servicing 70,000 policies. I imagine that is a fairly average ratio of staff and organization to the volume of business.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
If we are concerned, Mr. Chairman, with ensuring that the Canadian people are able to acquire protection against the various hazards of life in a modern society as listed here such as fires, aircraft accidents, automobile accidents, boiler insurance, credit insurance, earthquake insurance, explosion insurance and the whole list right down to the end, windstorm insurance, then I think we have to examine the question of whether or not we can provide them with protection from these vicissitudes by means of competition or whether we should not seriously consider now that this particular type of service to the people of Canada should be carried on by a public authority at much less cost. Obviously it would be at much less cost.
It is impossible, I think, to make out any case whatever for the suggestion that competition is going to have the traditional effect in this particular field. Competition is bound inevitably to increase costs over the whole
Private Bills
insurance business. Competition is bound to increase premiums and increase the cost of insurance for those who seek protection.
I think it is the responsibility of this parliament to decide that this whole matter should be examined with very great care. I brought the matter up in the committee the other day, on another life insurance company bill sponsored by the same hon. member. I suggested then that the time had come for us to give serious consideration to the whole insurance business. The other aspect of the business that is important is that this bill would provide a means by which savings are accumulated. This is a sort of gambling operation. It is a gambling operation in which those who are running the house are able to ensure that they are never going to lose to any great extent.
Once in a while some major catastrophe occurs and one insurance company goes under in the storm, but that is a very rare occurrence. I would imagine, Mr. Chairman, that the very fact we have this endless string of new incorporations for every kind of insurance company indicates quite clearly that this is a very profitable business, that there is a great deal of profit to be gained out of protecting the Canadian people-from the innumerable accidents that may overtake them in our modern society. This being the case, sir, I think it is the responsibility of parliament to find out just how expensive this insurance is for the Canadian people and how these expenses may be reduced.
I want to return for a moment, if I may, to the question of foreign ownership of these institutions. I point out that only in the last two days we have had an example of one of the dangers of foreign ownership, about which no satisfactory answer was received. I may say, from spokesmen on behalf of the government.
I want to stress the fact that two ministers of finance have suggested that foreign ownership of financial institutions in Canada is not conducive to the Canadian welfare. Here in this bill we are providing the opportunity for a completely foreign owned corporation to gamble with the Canadian people, to extract from the Canadian people premiums to cover possible losses. The company may transmit its profits out of this country to the detriment of our balance of payments problem. I have often wondered, Mr. Chairman, when I am told that we must have great infusions of foreign capital in order to keep our economy going, if perhaps we stopped some of these

July 14, 1966
Private Bills
leaks-they are getting to be very large leaks now-which may run into the hundreds of millions of dollars per year we might find ourselves in the happy position of not having to rely, and it is a dangerous reliance, on these infusions of foreign capital. There may be a case that can be made out for foreign investment in productive enterprises. There can be, I submit, no case whatever made out for giving a licence to people who are not Canadians, people who are foreign to this country, to gamble with the Canadian people and extract from the Canadian people part of their income in order to protect those people from accidents.
This is something that should be undertaken by Canadians, only by Canadians, and preferably by Canadians jointly and collectively through their publicly elected governmental bodies. Otherwise, it means we are deciding against the interests of the mass of the Canadian people in favour of not merely our own privileged groups but the privileged groups of another country. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that the time has come to examine what the costs are in these companies. I have a note here held over from an earlier debate on this bill and it states that the costs are 10 per cent to 30 per cent. I do not know if the hon. member who is sponsoring this bill has figures on this point, but I am not really concerned whether he has. In an operation of this size I am concerned only with the volume of profits that must be transmitted across the border year by year as this company continues to operate with a licence from the parliament of Canada.
Again I suggest to you, sir, it is the duty of those of us who are here representing the Canadian people, not representing special interests either native or foreign, to make sure that when the Canadian people want to protect themselves from accidents of all sorts they should have coverage at the cheapest possible rates. At the same time we should be able to ensure that there is no unnecessary drain on the resources of this country which such a company constitutes. This, I believe, is a very serious matter. I should like to see all these insurance bills stood over until there is a proper investigation of the whole insurance business in Canada because I have been convinced-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDINGS OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Nicholson for the second reading of Bill No. C-215, respecting certain conditions of employment of dock workers at the ports of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Lewis.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDINGS OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-215 is unjust and mischievous and to permit its passage would bring great discredit upon parliament. The bill will bring discredit upon individuals in this government who never again would be accepted as honest brokers in labour disputes between management and labour. As we know, Mr. Speaker, a great deal of labour unrest still faces this country and government will be forced to take action to deal with it.
[DOT] (7:00 p.m.)
Second, it will bring discredit upon the supporters of the government, because by supporting this bill they betray the origins of liberalism, or they forfeit the trust that they should have in their leaders. For their leaders said nearly the exact converse of the philosophy espoused by the bill, almost until the very last moment before it was introduced.
Third, to pass Bill No. C-215 would bring discredit upon the whole institution of parliament. For as the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) pointed out so ably, we are being asked to give a blank endorsement to the placement in the labour contract which now exists of terms and conditions which would be drawn up by a commissioner, without there being any opportunity for either of the two sides involved to alter so much as one small fraction of any of those terms and conditions. People would ask: Why on earth do parliamentarians behave as donkeys, passing such legislation?
Years ago, Mr. Speaker, we had a member of this chamber who, after various unsuccessful voyagings in Saskatchewan, has now found his way to the other place. Once in comment on some notion expressed by a member of the Liberal opposition of the day he said: "This is the most unheard of thing I have ever heard of". I did not agree with him at that time, but when Bill No. C-215 wanders into his hands tonight in the other place-presuming it passes here-then he can repeat that sentence and I will agree with him fully.
July 14. 1966

It is possible, Mr. Speaker, under the powers that will be conferred upon the commissioner, whose report will be final and will become part of the contract, to stretch things to the absurd length, for example, of requiring that unloading on the longshores of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec city be carried out by elephants or camels. According to my reading of one clause it might be possible that he would require the longshoremen to do their work in bikinis in the middle of winter.
I do not suggest that the commissioner would abuse the powers that are placed in his hands with such absurd recommendations, Mr. Speaker, but I do suggest this: The power that we would be giving to the commissioner by passage of this bill would surely inhibit any person. I do not think that any one of us would ever like to feel that a commissioner had the last word on anything. There must exist the right for larger bodies or for other people to consider his actions.
I say that this places the commissioner, who perforce by this bill becomes a compulsory arbitrator, in an impossible position. It will also do this to him: No matter what his recommendations, people will be aggrieved by them. Some of those people will be unkind enough to suggest that this was part of the deal beforehand, that it was very well known that the commissioner was going to bring in such recommendations and that this was part of some under-the-table scheme. I am sure that this situation does not exist either, but none the less Mr. Commissioner Picard is put in that position. Therefore I say that Bill No. C-215 will promote mischief. It will lower the esteem of parliament and it will go a long way toward destroying what is left of the ability of this particular government to govern effectively in a time of labour unrest.
The hon. member for Ontario has stated clearly and unequivocally that we cannot condone or support compulsory arbitration; and I repeat the statement that he made then, so that our stand is quite clear. I think I can also say on behalf of my party that we will support the position set forth in the amendment moved by the New Democratic Party; and at the conclusion of my speech I will suggest three, four or five alternatives by which the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) could act and take parliament from the unholy position in which it is now placed.
We have had the advantage, Mr. Speaker, of the intervention by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Marchand),
Labour Conditions
who late in the day enters upon the scene. He said-and very fairly too-that he would not want to replace the Minister of Labour in the negotiations, and I am quick to add that I would not want to see him replace the Minister of Labour in the negotiations either. But he could have sat in with the Minister of Labour, who had the advantage-whatever it was-of the help of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) and various others. Why not have gone to an expert who has made labour mediation his whole life's work, instead of bringing in those who have had very little experience with the subject?
When the minister defended, as he tried to do, compulsory arbitration, he confused methods of arbitration agreed to by parties well before any dispute arose. He did that at one time; at another time he confused the issue that is now before us with compulsory arbitration as set forth in the general laws of this country. As he well knows, and as we in this house all know, the compulsory arbitration which is being brought into this particular dispute is something smuggled in at the last minute, after everybody's attention had been diverted with many glowing statements about the virtues of collective bargaining. I regret that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, for whom I have a great deal of respect, has lost the candour for which he is famous, and on this particular occasion has adopted the dialectic used by others in the cabinet.
Before I review the record-and I will call this a "review B.C.": "before compulsion"-let me say this: I have a small apology to make to the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) before I read some of the glowing statements made on this matter by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and some others. I read his contribution on this particular matter during the labour estimates and found it very difficult to understand. I have read it a couple of times and I cannot understand it. I think what happened is this. He was trying to bring "Industry and Humanity" up to date, but failed. Why? Well, my theory is that the custodian of the crystal ball, the Minister of Transport, dropped it at some time somewhere, and the message did not get through from the great beyond.
First, referring to the exchange between the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) and the minister, as set forth at page 5636 of Hansard for May 27:

speechtext:
...Has consideration been given by his department to the use of compulsory arbitration as a means of setting disputes, rather than

July 14. 1966
Labour Conditions
resorting to strike action, as has been the case for many years?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDINGS OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
...Very serious consideration has been given to this matter by the department and by experienced departmental officials over a period of several years. As a member of cabinet I know something of the difficulties that we have had in trying to work out and find an acceptable formula. If you really believe, as I happen to, in the importance and the significance of collective bargaining, which enables management and labour to sit down on opposite sides of the table and unburden their hearts and take strong positions if necessary, it is difficult to say in all cases compulsory arbitration would be necessary, or advisable.
Then the minister makes remarks concerning national interest, safety and security, for example in the air lines industry, movement of passengers and freight, in many cases on the railways; and then he says this:
I cannot give the hon. member a definite answer, but I can assure him-and this is why I made the appeal earlier today-that any constructive suggestions, which any member of this house or any other person may have to make as to how we might solve this extremely difficult question, when our national interests and economy are at stake, would be very welcome.
A constructive suggestion came from the former minister of labour, the hon. member for Ontario, on May 31, as reported at page 5743 of Hansard, when he asked:
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
-Will the Prime Minister call the parties involved to Ottawa, to bring them into a different atmosphere so they may proceed to a settlement through the collective bargaining arrangement, under the chairmanship of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Marchand), who has a great deal of experience in this type of work?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDINGS OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, everything that can be done is being done to bring this strike to an end. The Minister of Labour is in touch with the situation, as my hon. friend knows, and if and when the time comes that the minister who is dealing with the matter feels the intervention of the Prime Minister would be helpful, naturally he will let me know.
Those words were said after the strike had been going on for some time. The strike was causing considerable confusion to the economy in Montreal, Trois-Rivieres, Quebec city, and perforce in the rest of the country.
Then we have this question by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) at page 6054 of Hansard:
Can the Prime Minister tell us whether his government anticipates bringing in legislation to end the strike on the St. Lawrence seaway, in view of its prolonged duration and in view of the statement made by the Minister of Finance?
I interject parenthetically that the statement by the Minister of Finance dealt with

the effect of the strike on grain shipments. The Prime Minister answered by saying:
Mr. Speaker, we hope this strike will be ended shortly by the process of free collective bargaining.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDINGS OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
We have here the statement of the Prime Minister and the performing mice.
The record continues on June 9, at page 6173, where the Prime Minister says:
-We have not by any means given up hope that this serious issue will be settled very shortly by the processes of free collective bargaining and not by parliamentary direction.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDINGS OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Continuing, on June 10 at page 6240 the Minister of Labour says:
Mr. Speaker, if I remember the right hon. Prime Minister's words yesterday, he said the government was hopeful, as a result of recent developments, that a settlement would be brought about through collective bargaining in good faith with a sincere desire on the part of both parties to see an end to the dispute.
Then we have this intervention of the former minister of labour, now the Minister of National Health and Welfare, on June 13 at page 6907:
We have here a system of free collective bargaining, and it is the earnest endeavour of the government to reach a solution to these difficult labour situations through the procedures which have been established by law under that system of free collective bargaining.
Then came perhaps the happiest moment that the minister has had-I do not think he has had many since-when he announced what we all thought was the final settlement of this particular issue. Following the statements made, the hon. member for Burna-by-Coquitlam made an observation which I shall read. It is to be found at page 6369 of Hansard for June 14, as follows:
I certainly have no objection to the idea of setting up a commission of inquiry to look into this matter, providing the decisions and recommendations of that commission are not binding upon both parties but are simply for the purpose of providing a basis upon which collective bargaining negotiations may continue. I hope the minister will give us some more information about that, perhaps when the orders of the day are called.
Earlier the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) had stated that the members of his party were very happy that a solution had been found without the necessity for parliamentary intervention. He said this:
Perhaps the proposal we made last week for parliamentary intervention without compulsory arbitration may have had some bearing on bringing the parties together.
July 14, 1966

Labour Conditions
At no time had the Minister of Labour said: Well, we have an agreement, but there are two words in it, namely "or otherwise" which can bring about a bill. If there were any reservations in the minister's mind, they were not stated.
Continuing the record, on June 23 at page 6785 the Minister of Labour announced the appointment of Dr. Laurent Picard, under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, as a commissioner. There is no suggestion in the announcement that the findings of the commissioner would become part of the labour agreement, through the measure to which we are now referring.
Continuing the story on June 29 at page 7019 we have the following:

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDINGS OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext: I wish to address a question to the Minister of Labour arising out of the bill he introduced earlier, and ask him to tell the house whether he informed the union or the shipping federation at the time the settle-men was reached of his intention to introduce compulsory arbitration of the issue of productivity, following the appointment of a commission of inauiry.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDINGS OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext: I most certainly did, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDINGS OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext: I wish to make sure of this. Did the minister inform both the union and the federation, or just one of those organizations?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF FINDINGS OF INDUSTRIAL COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Yes.
This was the first indication, of course, to my knowledge of a suggestion which had never been advanced in the press, or in any statements made inside or outside the house, that methods other than free collective bargaining were to be used in settling this particular dispute.
Continuing the story further, on July 8 at page 7387 the Minister of Labour said:
X think the phrase "compulsory arbitration" was carefully avoided; but the fact that there would be a binding solution, a recommendation to parliament-that legislation be enacted to make the terms binding, that is, the recommendations of the industrial inquiry commission on certain aspects-there is no question about that, Mr. Speaker.
I would say that the arguments this afternoon presented by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) and by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis ) have clearly brought that fact out.
What about the agreement itself, Mr. Speaker? It is set forth on page 7436 of Hansard for July 8. The words over which so much time has been spent namely "or otherwise" are set forth in this document. The pertinent part reads as follows:
The agreements terminating on December 31, 1965, shall be amended by incorporating therein
the terms of settlement set out above and these amended agreements shall remain in effect until December 31, 1967, unless amended by negotiations or otherwise.
We have had the voices of Philadelphia trilling in this chamber this afternoon, trying to explain that the words "or otherwise" do not encompass anything so wide sweeping and important as compulsory arbitration. May I add my own thoughts. I will not deal with the words "or otherwise" but instead I shall deal with the word "unless". The way I read this provision, it means that the agreement remains unless something is done. That is, the agreement as set forth here shall remain in effect unless something is done. That agreement deals with wages and some other matters, but certainly not with questions of productivity, and like matters which are the heart and soul of the measure we are now considering.
The record, I think, clearly indicates an understanding which led to a misunderstanding which, if properly spelled out, might have saved difficulties for both sides. Perhaps the longshoremen would not have accepted the idea of a binding report by a commissioner. Perhaps they would have accepted it. But to ask working men to take the words, "or otherwise", and construe them into a piece of legislation being solemnly enacted in the House of Commons and in the other place, to which royal assent might be given, is stretching the absurd into the impossible.
[DOT] (7:20 pjn.)
The agreement is neither flesh nor fowl, but bad red herring. Yet, Mr. Speaker, there is an obligation on us to rescue the government from its own follies if there is to be hope for labour peace in Canada this year, and if we are to restore the confidence of management and labour that they can come to this place, present their problems, and the government will offer the assistance of its Department of Labour, its skilled people, and even such skills as members of the government themselves possess, to bring industrial stability to a country that is badly in need of the same. Therefore I make some positive suggestions to the minister to help extricate him from the difficulties that he himself, or somebody else, plunged him into.
There is the suggestion of the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) to forsake the bill and leave it up to the two sides by collective bargaining or, at the very least, to let them look at the report of Mr. Commissioner Picard and make what they can of it before

July 14, 1966
Labour Conditions
coming back to parliament and telling us their troubles again.
Also, there is the suggestion made some time ago by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) which the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) considered although, to my knowledge, he did not act upon it. It is set forth at page 6299 of Hansard for June 13, when the Leader of the Opposition inquired- -whether the government is giving consideration to setting up a commission to review in detail the general position created in employer-employee relations by reason of technological change, a matter that is of prime importance in connection with the various disputes which are arising?
The answer of the Prime Minister was:
Mr. Speaker, the matter mentioned by my right hon. friend is, of course, one of very great and continuing significance, as we have learned

if we needed to learn-from the dispute that we have been discussing. It may well be, Mr. Speaker, that if the house requires an opportunity to discuss this particular dispute, this will be one of the elements that we will be discussing. I quite agree that it should be considered in its wider context. I think it would be the feeling of the house that the government would give consideration to an examination of the kind suggested by my right hon. friend.
I might add that the dispute being discussed at that particular time was the longshoremen dispute. That is the second suggestion I would mention which received an at-least-we-will-look-into-it-because-it-is-a-good-idea reply from the Prime Minister.
I would suggest to the minister that this is a way out for him not to deal with the longshore dispute by the compulsory arbitration set forth in this bill by having the broader issues examined, so that these people will not feel they are being treated separate or apart but that the whole problem of automation, job security and productivity is being examined at the same time. This could be done, as the Leader of the Opposition has suggested, by setting up a commission of inquiry, and to this I would add the suggestion that we could do it in yet another way.
I suggest we could refer these important issues of job security, automation and productivity-surely the most momentous issues now facing the business and industrial life of the country-to a committee of this house in which a large number of hon. members, coming from varied backgrounds, could examine all these things.
I myself have great faith, I will not call it optimistic faith but faith which I am sure would be justified, in what such a committee study could bring forth not only to help the disputants in this particular case but also to 
set guidelines, by legislation if need be, that would help labour disputants in this country over a generation ahead in dealing with problems caused by computers and all the other modern trappings.
These are several suggestions, in addition to the one offered by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) that the subject matter of the dispute be referred to a committee. In that respect our ideas are probably very much alike.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I say that the bill is unjust and mischievous. It will bring government, the supporters of government, and parliament itself into discredit. I want to make it clear that the Conservative opposition supports the amendment proposed by the hon. member for York South, and I also want to make it clear that we will reject Bill C-215.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the house understands why I want to take part in the discussion on that bill respecting conditions of employment at the ports on the St. Lawrence and on the amendment moved by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis).
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, before going on to my main remarks, I would like to thank all hon. members in my name and on behalf of all my constituents for the extreme courtesy and respect they show for the name of my riding, since I brought the matter up in the house, and the last example is that of the previous speaker who was careful to call my city Trois-Rivieres, as it should be called. Some people may think that it is an insignificant matter but in my riding it is a matter of pride, of family feeling, and saying that we are happy about the courtesy shown by my colleagues here is saying a lot.
About the bill, Mr. Speaker, I will say that, as an independent, I am a little like a spectator who does not even pay the amusement tax, who has the pleasure of seeing people in office introduce their bills and also seeing with what vigour the opposition fights them. I find it not only very entertaining but also very instructive.
For instance, I have great esteem for the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) and for the hon. member for York South, because they are never dull. They are above average speakers and also they have quite
July 14, 1966

an extraordinary gift for parliamentary debate; they always interest me even when 1 do not share their views.
I must say just the same that there are times when the strength of their arguments was greatly reduced in the eyes of the most interested spectator that I am, the independent spectator, by the partisan contingencies which become obvious. For instance, when I heard this afternoon the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) bitterly criticize the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) in a tone of voice and with arguments which seemed forced, twisted, in many cases, I said to myself, of course he is a member of the official opposition, leader of his party, he must absolutely object. That is his role, that of Her Majesty's loyal opposition, to object with all its might, with the argumentative strength at his disposal to what the government proposes.
In the eyes of the interested spectator as well as in those of probably many spectators outside this house, that weakens probably, certainly in many cases, the strength of his arguments. And that enables us to ask ourselves questions on the value, as far as sincerity is concerned, of some arguments voiced.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to tell a story about the member for York South (Mr. Lewis). I am known in my home town as one who likes to tease members of the bar, lawyers. Some people even say that I am allergic to lawyers. This may not be true. I like to tease them because lawyers can hit back better than other people. They are more argumentative.
Lawyers in several provinces of the country are great friends of mine. Back home, those whom I cruelly tease vote for me most of the time. But I was amazed in many cases at the reaction of some lawyers when I asked them, after hearing them making their plea with extraordinary conviction and eloquence: if, by any chance, the individual you defended crossed over to the other side and you had to put the case for the prosecutor, would you do it with as much conviction? And those lawyers would answer: Of course, it is my job. I must resort to all the tricks of the law to win my customer's case.
So then, Mr. Speaker, for a layman such as I, truth does not stem from legislation, but legislation from truth. With the years, I have reached the point where many questions come to my mind when I hear brilliant indictments
Labour Conditions
or eloquent pleas such as that of the hon. member for York South this afternoon. In his argument, he failed, in his wisdom and knowledge to consider that for common people such as me and many others, who heard him say "All my life I have been counsel for certain unions, I have appeared for certain unions" that would remind us: "He is doing his job and his job as a lawyer is to defend his client, the client who is paying his salary." I do not know whether he is still on the pay roll of the unions, but evil tongues claim that the N.P.D. campaign funds are supplied by-I am happy to see the hon. member for York South entering the house because I would have disliked to speak of him in his absence, I have too high a regard for him. The Holy Ghost probably inspired him to come and hear what I have to say and more power to him-when the member for York South brought out that point, the value of his argument was reduced to my layman's mind. And when I recalled that it is being unkindly said, although it may be true and it seems warranted by certain indications and by certain events, that the campaign funds of the N.P.D. are supplied by certain powerful unions, I may say that the value of his argument was somewhat reduced.
At home, Mr. Speaker, I am not being financed by any union although, to the surprise of the N.P.D., I would say that most of their supporters voted for the independent member, because the independent member for Trois-Rivieres has always told the truth to the union members at home. Twenty times, possibly, I negotiated collective agreements and I negotiated with learned lawyers, wise in the ways of labour-management relations, and we always got along fine.
We only had a dispute once, which involved a bastard union. I am not saying it was a bastard union: the other unions, the Conseil des metiers du travail, the Syndicats natio-naux catholiques clamoured from the roof tops that it was a bastard union. That is probably why we did not agree.
But, Mr. Speaker, I have always told the people back home, our union people with whom I have had contacts in public life for 20 years what I believed to be the truth.
After this preamble, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that, under the present circumstances, I fail to see how anyone can blame the minister for introducing this bill. When it is claimed that it deals a blow to free and

July 14, 1966
Labour Conditions
voluntary negotiations, I say the facts and the truth are being twisted. I say the best proof that the parties accepted that solution, when there was no other alternative, is that they decided to go back to work. There was, therefore, tacit agreement, Mr. Speaker.
And when they say that this is an almost criminal interference with free and voluntary bargaining, they forget that this is an exceptional case.
As for me, Mr. Speaker, I would go farther than the Minister of Labour. I submit that, in public services or in organizations, even those not directly responsible for public service, but having contingencies where public interest is at stake, there should be a machinery to provide for prompt bargaining. For instance, it should be provided that three, four or five months before the expiry of a collective agreement, the parties concerned should sit down and negotiate. And if on expiry of the collective agreement, for instance, they did not agree, let us have arbitration courts to settle the matter.
After all, in our complex economy we must manage to arrive at some sensible solution. I tell you that it is not intelligent to allow a union to endanger the whole economy of a country to satisfy its own interest.
And I am not the only one to say so, Mr. Speaker. I should like to advance the testimony of someone who knows more about it than I, because I did some research when, like everyone, I read in the papers what the president of the Labour Congress said at one time. The Montreal La Presse said:
The president of the Canadian Labour Congress violently contested yesterday the statements of the Minister of Labour who said that compulsory arbitration could help to reduce the number of strikes.
Mr. Jodoin added:
However, he said, if union members are to keep their integrity and share in Canada's growing prosperity-
I find that very surprising. In order to share in the growing prosperity, we must jeopardize it by ruinous strikes such as we have known.
They must be able to stop working without threat of government intervention.
Elsewhere, Mr. Speaker, I found a statement by Mr. Walter Reuther, president of the United Auto Workers, affiliated to the American Federation of Labor and to the C.I.O. He is not a newcomer in the field of labour; following the strike of the bus drivers in

New York a short time ago, he said this- I shall try to give as faithful a translation as possible and in case I do a bad job, I shall say I took this passage from the January or February issue of Time magazine: we must put an end to our strikes-this is Walter Reuther speaking-we must put an end to our strikes, which are endangering the survival of society. We can no longer tolerate a situation where a group of employees, even if they have a right to what they ask, can paralyse the economy of a whole community.
It is obvious that Walter Reuther is not in favour of compulsory arbitration. He suggests solutions less generous and less ruinous than endless strikes. In regard to protracted strikes which further the interests of some people, he adds this: We must create without delay a tripartite commission representing the worker, the employer and the state, which will set up the machinery for new policies for the immediate settling of strikes in the public service.
Well, I for one believe that the bill before us is not only acceptable but that it is going to provide, once and for all, for those disputes which are disastrous to the economy.
And I was shocked at hearing the hon. member for York South say: "Postpone that. And if another disastrous strike should occur, it will still be time to pass legislation."
We would have to go through another disastrous strike, Mr. Speaker. For my part, I believe that workers have had more than enough of such things.
I suggest that our workers are getting to wonder whether this is not all eye-wash, whether the whole truth is not hidden from them. I think it is time that workers in 1966 hear the truth, even from their politicians, even from their labour leaders, even from the learned lawyers representing the labour union. In a case such as the one with which we are concerned, at a time when an agreement could not be reached, I say that the will of both parties was expressed clearly enough to warrant government action. I would go as far as to say that the government waited too long to take action and, in saying that, I say I have the support of the rank and file of the labour unions, perhaps not of the leaders whose prestige is at stake if they accept that, but of the people who have to tighten their belts when they have been on strike for 38 or 40 days without getting any wages.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the workers are wondering whether too many people are not
July 14. 1966

playing politics with the workers' interests and with the so-called benefits of labour unions. I think that the workers are beginning to realize that they are being fooled in order to increase the prestige of some fabulously paid labour leaders.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that the workers are aware of the fact that they are the ones to foot the final bill on all disputes harmful to the whole economy and that they may be the cat's-paw, in other words, the suckers. They are too well informed these days, not to realize that the wool is being pulled over their eyes and they are only waiting for the opportunity to rightly rebel against such goings-on. They have not had many opportunities so far and I know something about it, because I have personally walked the docks of Trois-Rivieres for twenty years. I have in Montreal and also in Quebec, a certain number of friends and acquaintances who give me their views on the situation and tell me, each in turn, that they would refuse, in certain circumstances, to follow their labour leaders if they were not being threatened with broken legs or being thrown into the St. Lawrence. For the enlightenment of those who think that I am dreaming this up, let me remind them of all that happened a few years back at the time of Hal Bank's union and what came out at the inquiry that the government launched later to find out what had occurred.
I say that our workers find it intolerable to see labour leaders urging them to break the law, to overlook court orders and to flout the law, because their own interests are involved, knowing that this will boomerang, that others will also scorn the law and that they, themselves, will become the victims of such contempt of law.
Mr. Speaker, under the circumstances, I think it is the government's duty to take action, which it did perhaps a little too late, in my opinion. Maybe it did not have the freedom to do it before, obviously fearing all this public protest coming from certain sectors more concerned about their personal advantage than about the commonwealth, but this is a case where the government cannot forget that the commonwealth must come before everything, that the general economy of the nation must have precedence even over the rightful interest of a group, and I think that our workers have enough common sense to understand it.
Mr. Speaker, our workers want to work; they want the government to give them work 23033-487J
Labour Conditions
or organize an economy where they can find employment. They want to work at reasonable wages and for that, they know that the economy must be strong, firm. There are no miracles in life and they know it. They are sufficiently well-informed nowadays to know that. It is no longer possible to make them believe that the moon is made of green cheese and they know that, at times, the government will have to intervene to protect them and that, in other cases, it will have to bring them to reason because they will have been misled by others. I think the majority of our workers are eagerly seeking that truth and that they will be happy to see that the government has the courage of its responsibilities.
Mr. Speaker, I know it is unpopular to speak this way. I am also of the opinion that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) know very well that after the statements they made there will be tomorrow a general outcry in certain fanatic and pro-labour papers and when I say prolabour, I mean in a fanatic way, because there are papers which are pro-labour in an intelligent way. Hence, that calls for certain courage. I know also that my statements will perhaps not be popular in a certain press but I know that they reflect the feeling of the humble worker who is deprived of his wages during three or four weeks because of legal red tape and of bickering on the meaning of a word or of a sentence which enable learned lawyers to get phenomenal salaries and politicians to make the fortune of their political party, while they do not have the means to pay for their groceries during the week end.
Mr. Speaker, I will vote in favour of the bill and against the amendment of the New Democratic Party for the reasons that I have outlined and for others that I would have liked to point out. But I do not want to overtax the patience of the house, I will conclude my remarks now and repeat the words of a famous politician named Abraham Lincoln, for the benefit of those who deal with labour questions in a biased or interested manner:
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)

You can fool some of the people some of the time, and some of the people all of the time, but you can't fool all of the people all of the time.

speechtext:
That is a regrettable situation, but it is what hon. gentlemen opposite are asking us to do. I for one think this is an extreme misuse of the rules of this house. Unfortunately this misuse will continue so long as the government blindly insists on ramming this bill through parliament, and so long as the government refuses to accept the cautious course advocated by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) in his amendment.
If hon. members opposite would accept our advice and proceed cautiously in regard to this bill, permitting the subject matter to go to a committee before which hon. gentlemen here, Mr. Jodoin and Mr. Cutler could appear as witnesses, perhaps the committee could come to a conclusion as to the facts. The key to the whole matter is, as has been said by many hon. members and by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, who said what, and who agreed to what? I quite frankly say this, with all due respect to the rules and the minister, that at this juncture I am not prepared to accept the minister's version as to what took place, because on a number of occasions when he has spoken in this house about this matter he has hedged, qualified and been vague.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
I think in a situation such as this, perhaps unique in labour-management history, perhaps unique in parliamentary history, that was no time for the Minister of Labour to be coy. It was no time for him to be silent about this extremely vital question of whether or not there should be compulsory arbitration. I should like to read what the minister said, as have other hon. members. On June 14 the
July 14, 1966

minister announced the settlement of the dispute. I shall read only the particularly relevant sections of his remarks. I do not want to read them out of context, and if anybody wants me to read the whole thing, I will do so. He said, as reported at page 6368:
It was difficult if not impossible for the parties to agree on the nature and extent of possible increases of productivity.
He was there approaching the nub of this question. Then he said:
When this situation developed I, as Minister of Labour, several weeks ago announced that I intended to set up a commission of inquiry under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act to inquire into the possibilities of improving productivity-
That was the time the minister should have disclosed that he was going to do something unique. This was the time that I contend the minister misled the house by not going further, by not saying that he really did not intend to set up a commission under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act as it exists. He should have said: We intend to follow that up by introducing legislation which will make that commissioner's report final and binding. He did not say that at that time.

I now wish to confirm that I intend to set up such a commission within the next few days. I will have more to say on that subject when I announce the appointment of the commissioner.

something in addition to the mere appointment of a commissioner under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. I submit that the minister was probably ashamed to say it at that time-
